papers.title: Seasonal and daily rhythms in healthy adults and individuals with obesity: associations with selected hormones and lifestyle factors.
papers.abstract: Biological timing systems, including circadian and seasonal rhythms, play a key role in regulating human physiology. The central circadian "body clock," located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, coordinates daily rhythms both centrally and via peripheral clocks in metabolic tissues. Seasonal rhythms, in turn, are shaped by environmental cues such as photoperiod and temperature and may influence mood, appetite, sleep, physical activity, hormonal secretion, and thermoregulation. Although seasonal responses are generally weaker in humans than in many other animals, evidence suggests that some physiological processes remain seasonally regulated. From a physiological anthropology perspective, these rhythms can be viewed as adaptive mechanisms that align human physiology and behavior with predictable environmental changes. These timing systems are increasingly recognized as important regulators of metabolic homeostasis. Disruption of circadian and seasonal rhythms may contribute to insulin resistance, altered energy expenditure, fat accumulation, and obesity-related dysfunction. Human studies suggest that biological timing is reflected in chronotype-related behaviors, endocrine responses, seasonal hormonal variation, and thermoregulatory adaptation. Obesity is a complex, multifactorial disease that cannot be explained solely by excessive energy intake and low physical activity. It develops through interactions between external factors, such as an unhealthy diet and a sedentary lifestyle, and internal factors, including genetic, metabolic, endocrine, and behavioral mechanisms. Therefore, obesity should be understood not only as a disorder of energy balance but also as a condition influenced by disrupted biological timing. This article builds on our 2015 review (Kanikowska et al., Int J Biometeorol 59:377-84, 2015) by synthesizing recent literature and emerging perspectives on the roles of circadian and seasonal rhythms in obesity.

papers.title: Resting-state EEG features of cognitive fluctuations across the Lewy body disease spectrum.
papers.abstract: Cognitive fluctuations (CF) are a core feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) that negatively impact quality of life. Despite their prevalence and negative impact, CF are challenging to identify clinically. The goal of this study was to identify easily obtainable EEG features associated with CF across the spectrum of Lewy body disease (LB). We conducted a cross-sectional study of 53 patients prospectively enrolled through the outpatient clinics of the Department of Neurology at Virginia Commonwealth University. Based on the Clinician Assessment of Fluctuations, participants were categorized as LB disease without CF (LB-CF) or LB disease with CF (LB + CF). All participants underwent a resting-state EEG recording with eyes closed for at least 3 min. EEG data were preprocessed and the following features were extracted: dominant frequency (DF), dominant frequency variability (DFV), dominant frequency prevalence (DFP), and individual alpha peak frequency (IAF). We applied Kruskal-Wallis tests and logistic regression models to evaluate differences in EEG features between study groups. We analyzed EEG features for 29 LB + CF and 24 LB-CF participants. Compared to the LB-CF group, the LB + CF group had significantly lower DF, DFP-alpha, and IAF in all derivations (all p < 0.05). In logistic regression analysis adjusting for age, sex, and MoCA score, these EEG features remained significant predictors of group (LB + CF vs. LB-CF, all q < 0.05). The elastic-net logistic regression model identified five predictors (anterior DFP-alpha, anterior DFP-pre-alpha, anterior DF, temporal DF, and temporal IAF) achieving an AUC of 0.86, whereas anterior DFP-alpha alone achieved an AUC of 0.85. Among patients with LB disease, resting-state EEG features were associated with CF and were significant predictors of CF even after adjustment for age, sex, and MoCA. The development of an EEG-based biomarker of CF using this set of features could improve diagnosis of Lewy body dementia.

papers.title: Diabetes and all-cause mortality in a national telemonitored heart failure cohort: role of comorbidities, heart failure etiology burden, and short-term weight variability.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is common in patients with heart failure (HF) and is associated with worse outcomes. However, its prognostic role in real-world telemonitored HF populations remains insufficiently characterized. We evaluated the association between diabetes and all-cause mortality in a national telemonitored HF cohort while considering HF severity, comorbidities, HF etiology burden, and short-term weight variability (WV). We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults enrolled in the French Satelia® Cardio telemonitoring program between 2018 and 2024 (NCT07561866). Baseline clinical characteristics, HF etiologies, comorbidities, and repeated weight measurements were analyzed. Short-term WV was defined as the mean absolute 10-day weight change per patient and categorized according to the cohort median. Survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analyses and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Among 16,556 patients (mean age 74.9 ± 12.9 years; 64% male), 4,723 (28.5%) had diabetes. Median follow-up was 13 months in patients with diabetes and 11 months in those without diabetes; 2,266 patients died (13.7%). Patients with diabetes more frequently had ischemic and hypertensive HF etiologies, obesity and greater HF etiology burden. In multivariable models without NYHA class, diabetes was independently associated with higher mortality, with a significant diabetes-by-age interaction suggesting a stronger association among patients aged < 75 years. After adjustment for NYHA class in the smaller subgroup, this association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant. Male sex, clinician-reported renal failure, combined chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and sleep apnea syndrome, and higher NYHA class were associated with higher mortality, whereas obesity was associated with lower mortality. Individual HF etiologies were not consistently associated with mortality across adjusted models, whereas increasing HF etiology burden remained associated with higher mortality. High short-term WV was associated with poorer survival. In this large national telemonitored HF cohort, the association between diabetes and mortality was attenuated after accounting for HF severity assessed by NYHA class. Mortality was more consistently associated with HF severity, comorbidities and cumulative HF etiology burden than with individual HF etiologies. Short-term WV emerged as an exploratory telemonitoring-derived marker associated with poorer survival. These findings support a multidimensional approach to risk assessment in patients with diabetes.

papers.title: Risk factor control and type 2 diabetes event risks in people with high genetic susceptibility to diabetes.
papers.abstract: To explore whether the excess risk of type 2 diabetes (T2D) attributable to genetic predisposition could be mitigated by controlling modifiable risk factors and whether this mitigation is attenuated in individuals with prediabetes. We included 382,313 participants from the UK Biobank for T2D analyses. The main exposure was the number of optimally controlled risk factors including non-smoker, high level of physical activity, healthy diet, healthy sleep, low BMI, and non-hypertension. Genetic risk groups were defined as low and high categories based on a median of the T2D polygenic risk score. Cox proportional hazard models were employed to explore the associations of joint risk factor control with T2D. During a median of 13.5 years of follow-up, 9210 incident T2D cases were identified in the high genetic risk group. Among individuals with high genetic risk, those who achieved control of all six risk factors had a lower incidence of T2D than those with low genetic risk (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.79, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.68, 0.92). However, even with all six risk factors were controlled, participants with prediabetes still had a higher risk of developing T2D, compared with those who had low genetic risk and normal glucose levels. Our results indicated that optimal risk factor control may mitigate the genetic-related excess risk of T2D, but it cannot fully mitigate the prediabetes-related risk of T2D.

papers.title: Neural mechanisms underlying theory of mind application deficits in bipolar mania: an event-related potential study.
papers.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) impairment is observed in bipolar disorder (BD) across mood states and may be more pronounced during manic episodes. However, the neurophysiological basis of ToM application-particularly the temporal relationship between posterior perspective-related processing and later frontal processing during perspective selection and conflict management-remains poorly understood. Nineteen patients who met ICD-10 criteria for a bipolar manic episode and twenty-four healthy controls completed a rapid ToM judgment task while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Manic symptoms in the patient group were subthreshold according to established YMRS cutoffs at the time of assessment. Behavioral performance and event-related potentials (ERPs) were analyzed. The TP450 component (325-525 ms), associated with posterior perspective-related processing, and the Late Frontal Slow Wave (LFSW; 600-800 ms), treated as a marker of later frontal processing during perspective selection and conflict management, were examined. Compared with healthy controls, patients with BD showed reduced accuracy and prolonged reaction times across all conditions. ERP analyses revealed significantly attenuated TP450 amplitudes at right parietal sites (P4) in the BD group, consistent with altered posterior perspective-related processing. Patients also exhibited reduced LFSW amplitudes at left frontal sites (F3), consistent with altered recruitment of later frontal processes during the task. In this small clinical sample, the findings provide preliminary evidence for differences in posterior perspective-related processing and subsequent frontal processing during ToM application. The results require replication in larger, independent samples before they can be generalized to the broader population of patients with bipolar disorder. Not applicable.

papers.title: Navigating the diagnostic challenges of maladaptive daydreaming: a case report of ego-syntonic and ego-dystonic obsessive fantasies with functional impairment in a 17-year-old.
papers.abstract: Maladaptive daydreaming (MD) is an emerging and insufficiently recognized clinical phenomenon characterized by immersive fantasy activity associated with functional impairment. Its overlap with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and schizophrenia spectrum conditions creates significant diagnostic uncertainty, particularly in adolescents. We report the case of a 17-year-old female presenting with intrusive celebrity-focused fantasies, sleep disturbance, behavioral regression, social withdrawal, and reduced self-care. She described co-existing ego-syntonic and ego-dystonic obsessive imagery with auditory-like pseudo-hallucinatory experiences. The Maladaptive Daydreaming Scale (MDS-16) score was 76%, consistent with probable MD. Extensive medical and neuroimaging investigations were unremarkable. Differential diagnoses included OCD, schizotypal traits, ASD, and schizophrenia prodrome. Initial treatment with fluoxetine was changed to quetiapine, alongside cognitive behavioral therapy, occupational therapy, structured behavioral strategies, and family psychoeducation. The patient demonstrated gradual improvement in distress, insight, sleep, and engagement, although intrusive fantasies persisted. This case highlights the complexity of distinguishing MD from other psychiatric conditions in adolescents and supports the value of a multidisciplinary, function-focused management approach. Early recognition may prevent misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment. Not applicable.

papers.title: Physical activity in Swedish 3-year-old children: associations with lifestyle and behavioral factors.
papers.abstract: Physical activity (PA) positively affects children's health and well-being. Despite numerous studies on factors that influence PA in adults and older school-children, limited information exists about lifestyle factors, behavior, and neurodevelopmental predictors of PA in preschool children. This study aimed to (i) quantify the time spent in various activity levels (vigorous, moderate, light, and sedentary) among 3-year-old Swedish children, and (ii) examine associations between actigraphy-measured PA and various lifestyle, behavioral factors, and health in this age group. PA levels were measured using wrist-worn movement sensors (MotionWatch 8) in 497 3-year-old children in the ongoing NorthPop Birth Cohort in Northern Sweden. Motion data were collected over 24 h per day for eight continuous days and were classified into sleep, sedentary behavior, and PA intensities according to an age-, epoch-, and position-validated method. Children's lifestyle, health, and demographic data were collected using register data and parental questionnaires. Neurodevelopment and behavior were assessed using the Ages & Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) and Strength and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), respectively. Swedish 3-year-old children spent an average of 163 min on moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) per day. Boys spent significantly more time at MVPA levels than girls (p < 0.001). Children with better gross motor function, older siblings in the household, and spending more time playing outdoors demonstrated longer time spent at higher levels of PA over 24 h per day. Children with hyperactivity problems were more physically active, whereas those with peer problems had lower PA levels. Children who were exposed to more time playing on computer/phone spent less time being physically active. Three-year-olds in Sweden are generally highly active, with nearly all (99%) meeting the WHO recommendation of at least 60 min of MVPA per day and all (100%) meeting the recommendation of at least 180 min of total daily physical activity. The explanatory factors associated with particular PA levels are multidimensional, but the results suggest that behaviors such as playing outdoors and spending less time playing on computers/phones are associated with higher PA levels in this age group. Retrospectively registered at Researchweb 11 November 2024 (project number 279272).

papers.title: Sleep problem profiles, hyperactivity-inattention, and psychosocial health among high-altitude preschool children.
papers.abstract: Sleep is closely related to children's behavioral regulation and psychosocial functioning, yet preschool sleep is multidimensional and may vary substantially between children. High-altitude residence provides a distinctive ecological context for studying sleep. However, little is known about heterogeneity in measured sleep characteristics among preschool children living at high altitude, or how such heterogeneity relates to behavioral and psychosocial adjustment. This study identified sleep-problem profiles among high-altitude preschool children and examined their associations with hyperactivity-inattention, psychosocial health, and other adjustment outcomes. This cross-sectional study included 244 preschool children from Lhasa, Xizang, China (approximately 3,650 m). Caregiver-reported sleep indicators included six sleep-problem dimensions and weekday and weekend sleep duration. Latent profile analysis identified sleep-problem profiles. Multivariable logistic regression examined correlates of profile membership. Profile differences in behavioral difficulties, health-related quality of life, and academic achievement were examined. Hierarchical regression was further used to examine whether hyperactivity-inattention was associated with psychosocial health after accounting for sleep-profile membership and covariates. Two sleep-problem profiles were identified: a lower sleep-problem profile and a higher sleep-problem profile. Being an only child was associated with higher odds of membership in the higher sleep-problem profile, whereas daily screen time was not significantly associated with profile membership. Compared with children in the lower sleep-problem profile, those in the higher sleep-problem profile showed higher hyperactivity-inattention and lower psychosocial health. No significant profile differences were found for physical health or academic achievement. In hierarchical regression, hyperactivity-inattention was negatively associated with psychosocial health, and the association between sleep-profile membership and psychosocial health was attenuated but remained significant after hyperactivity-inattention was included. Two profiles differing primarily in overall sleep-problem severity were identified among high-altitude preschool children. The higher sleep-problem profile was associated with poorer behavioral and psychosocial adjustment but not with concurrent academic achievement. Hyperactivity-inattention may be an important behavioral correlate of poorer psychosocial functioning among children with higher sleep problems.

papers.title: Haptoglobin is associated with nocturnal blood pressure non-dipping in children with chronic kidney disease.
papers.abstract: Blood pressure (BP) follows a circadian rhythm that depends partly on endothelial nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability. Cell-free hemoglobin rapidly scavenges NO, and haptoglobin functions as a capacity-limited plasma buffer facilitating hemoglobin clearance. Whether reduced circulating haptoglobin contributes to circadian rhythm-related vascular dysregulation in pediatric chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains unclear. Sixty children with CKD were enrolled, and plasma haptoglobin levels were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Twenty-five participants underwent 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring. Nocturnal systolic BP non-dipping was defined as <10% decline in nighttime values. Multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Restricted cubic spline modeling assessed dose-response patterns. Fifteen of 25 children (60%) exhibited nocturnal non-dipping. Plasma haptoglobin levels were significantly lower in non-dippers than in dippers. Each 10 mg/dL increase in haptoglobin was independently associated with lower odds of non-dipping (adjusted OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.49-0.99; p = 0.044). Spline modeling suggested a threshold-like increase in risk at lower concentrations. Lower circulating haptoglobin is independently associated with nocturnal BP non-dipping in children with CKD. These findings suggest that reduced hemoglobin-buffering capacity may contribute to impaired circadian BP regulation, although mechanistic confirmation is required.

papers.title: Prevalence and factors associated with ambulatory blood pressure phenotypes in a semi-urban Nigerian population.
papers.abstract: Office blood pressure (BP) measurement alone may underestimate the true burden of abnormal BP regulation, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) remains underutilised. This study characterised the distribution and sociodemographic factors of ABPM-derived hypertension phenotypes in a semi-urban Nigerian population. This community-based cross-sectional study enrolled 348 adults in Ido-Ekiti, Nigeria, who underwent 24-hour ABPM alongside standardised office BP measurement. Phenotypes (white-coat, masked, sustained hypertension, and true normotension) and circadian abnormalities (nocturnal and morning hypertension) were classified using 2024 European Society of Hypertension thresholds. Associations with sociodemographic and lifestyle factors were assessed using chi-square tests and multivariable logistic regression. Sustained hypertension was present in 36.9% of participants, white-coat hypertension in 17.8%, masked hypertension in 5.0%, and true normotension in 40.3%. Nocturnal hypertension (56.8%) and morning hypertension (40.6%) were highly prevalent. Age showed the strongest and most consistent gradient across nearly all phenotypes (all P < 0.001), with sustained and nocturnal hypertension rising sharply and true normotension declining with advancing age. Female participants had significantly higher morning hypertension (46.4% vs. 33.3%, P = 0.013) and lower true normotension (29.6% vs. 41.0%, P = 0.025) than males. Monthly income showed phenotype-specific, non-uniform associations with sustained, morning, nocturnal hypertension, and true normotension, while showing no association with white-coat hypertension. ABPM revealed a substantial burden of abnormal BP patterns, particularly sustained, nocturnal and morning hypertension, with pronounced age-related variation. These findings support wider ABPM adoption in African clinical practice, while socioeconomic and behavioural associations should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than causal.

papers.title: Sleeping with the unknown: coronary vasospasm in an anomalous right circumflex artery mimicking in-stent restenosis.
papers.abstract: Coronary vasospasm represents a transient, reversible constriction of coronary arteries that often goes unrecognised in patients with established coronary artery disease or anomalous coronary anatomy. When combined with prior percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), vasospasm can closely mimic in-stent restenosis, leading to delayed diagnosis and unnecessary repeat interventions. We describe a 55-year-old male with prior PCI to an anomalous right circumflex artery (RCx) who presented with recurrent nocturnal chest pain and asymptomatic transient ST-segment elevation (STE) during sleep. Despite FFR-guided PCI to the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and subsequent repeat intervention for suspected RCx in-stent restenosis, symptoms persisted. A probable diagnosis of nocturnal coronary vasospasm was established based on the clinical presentation, characteristic nocturnal ECG changes, response to diltiazem, and exclusion of alternative structural pathology on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging; however, the diagnosis remains inferential in the absence of invasive provocation testing. This case illustrates the diagnostic complexity of probable coronary vasospasm in a male patient with structural coronary disease and anomalous coronary anatomy. Several factors may have contributed to diagnostic delay, including anchoring toward structural disease, angiographic ambiguity, anomalous anatomy, and the unusual nocturnal presentation. The differential response to calcium channel blocker subclasses in this patient is presented as a clinically relevant, hypothesis-generating observation rather than evidence of therapeutic superiority. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for probable coronary vasospasm in patients with recurrent nocturnal ST elevation following PCI, particularly when symptoms, telemetry findings, and coronary physiology are discordant with fixed obstructive disease. Careful reassessment, transparent acknowledgement of diagnostic uncertainty, and thoughtful use of non-invasive monitoring and targeted medical therapy may help avoid unnecessary repeat intervention.

papers.title: Transcriptomic analysis of flowers in an apple petalless mutant and its parents.
papers.abstract: Apple petals are required for insect pollination, and the number of petals is an important commercial trait for ornamental apples. Owing to the relatively small number of apple mutants, the molecular mechanism underlying flower organ development in apple remains unclear. A petalless apple mutant was discovered from hybrid seedlings of 'Wanbai' crabapple × 'Huayue'. Transcriptome analysis of the petalless mutant and its two parents was conducted. A total of 5,118 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified between flowers from 'Wanbai' crabapple and the petalless mutant (WBvsH), whereas 6,886 DEGs were identified between flowers from 'Huayue' and the petalless mutant (HYvsH). A total of 1,718 and 1,640 DEGs were co-upregulated and co-downregulated respectively, in the WBvsH and HYvsH comparison groups. KEGG analysis revealed that these co-upregulated DEGs were significantly enriched in plant hormone signal transduction, circadian rhythm-plant, and photosynthesis pathways, and these co-downregulated DEGs were significantly enriched in the biosynthesis of amino acids, carbon metabolism, and glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathways. Among these coregulated DEGs, compared with those in WB and HY, the expression of four organ identity class A genes, MdTOEL1, MdTOEL2, MdFUL2, and MdFUL1, and one organ identity class C gene, MdSTKL, were upregulated in H; the expression of three organ identity class B genes, MdAP3L1, MdAP3L2, and MdAP3L3, were downregulated in H; and the expression of the organ identity class E gene MdSEPL3 was upregulated, but the expression of MdSEPL1 and MdSEPL2 were downregulated. Yeast two-hybrid and split-luciferase complementation assays revealed that the class E protein MdSEPL1 promoted interactions between any two class B proteins; however, no interactions were detected between B proteins. This study provides comprehensive analysis of the gene expression in flowers of the two parents and the petalless mutant offspring to understand the mechanism of the formation of the petalless phenotype. In apple mutant, genes involved in auxin signaling pathway were activated and genes involved in primary metabolism pathways were inhibited. 3 floral organ identity-related AP3 orthologues were downregulated in apple mutant, suggesting that these genes may be candidate genes responsible for petal phenotype.

papers.title: Continuous multimodal neuromonitoring of zolpidem-induced paradoxical awakening in chronic incomplete locked-in syndrome: ventral pontine deafferentation, cross-modal complementarity, and cardio-cortical dissociation.
papers.abstract: Zolpidem paradoxically restores responsiveness in select disorders of consciousness (DOC) cases, yet real-time electrophysiological and autonomic dynamics across the pharmacodynamic trajectory remain uncharacterized in incomplete locked-in syndrome (LIS). A 52.18-min multimodal recording tracked baseline, enteral zolpidem administration (min 22.39), absorption, corticomotor peak, and plateau in a 42-year-old male with chronic LIS from pontine infarction. Analytics included continuous qEEG (0.5-70 Hz), microstates (Classes A-D), beta-band weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI) connectomics, heart rate variability (HRV), and heartbeat‑evoked responses (HER). Baseline deafferentation showed severe theta slowing (48.36 ± 4.14%) and phase hypersynchrony. Following enteral administration, the following changes were observed: 1. viscero-cortical dissociation: Infusion triggered an immediate HRV VHF surge (>80%) while the cortex remained quiescent for 14.1 min. 2. Corticomotor consolidation: Between min 36.5-46.0, relative beta surged (+266.89%) while theta dropped (-30.74%). Microstates accelerated into frontocentral Classes C/D, and connectomics demonstrated long-range edge pruning with selective frontocentral recruitment (wPLI > 0.40). 3. Interoceptive gating: During peak beta emergence, cardio-cortical communication collapsed; evoked global variance profile dropped > 60% (1.03 to 0.22 µV) alongside frontocentral dipole suppression. Paradoxical awakening is a coordinated multisystem process. Zolpidem disinhibits spared corticomotor networks while filtering ascending visceral baro-afferents, enabling an outward-facing behavioral state decoupled from internal interoception.

papers.title: The Transformative Role of Artificial Intelligence in Wearable Health Monitoring: Applications in Diagnosis, Therapy, and Rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: This chapter explores the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented wearable technology in dynamic health monitoring across diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation. Innovations include real-time cardiovascular disease detection, AI-driven continuous glucose monitoring for diabetes, and neurological disorder tracking using flexible electroencephalograph (EEG) sensors. Therapeutic advances feature smart drug-delivery patches responsive to biomarkers, remote intervention systems, and surgical tools like augmented reality (AR) navigation. Rehabilitation breakthroughs encompass wearables for motor recovery, cardiopulmonary optimization, and neurorehabilitation using brain-computer interfaces. Future progress hinges on multifunctional hardware, federated learning for privacy, explainable AI, and standardized regulations.

papers.title: Evaluation of a rapid batch export system for electroretinography waveform data.
papers.abstract: Accurate application of electroretinography (ERG) remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of retinal disorders. Despite its potential as a diagnostic tool, the clinical use of ERG is limited by the expertise required for interpretation and the error-prone manual extraction of waveform data. At scale, waveform analysis in academic research and clinical trials is made difficult by these challenges. This study performed external validation and quality assessment of automated compared to manual extraction and collection of raw ERG waveforms. Raw waveform data was collected using International Society for Clinical Electrophysiology of Vision (ISCEV) standard ERG studies from the ophthalmology practice at Columbia University. A recently developed automated batch exporting tool (Espion, Diagnosys LLC, Lowell, MA) was used to retrieve and compile data and compare with manually collected data for 357 patient sessions. The automated and manually exported data had 99.75% ± 0.17% similarity using a Jaccard similarity test, suggesting the automated tool is both rapid and highly accurate. We identified several inconsistencies leading to errors in the automated batch export. The most common errors in compiled batch exported data included: improperly merging two ERG files taken on the same day and lack of accounting for missing data. Use of batch export with manual oversight for sources of potential error can allow for faster, more effective data gathering and analysis of large-scale ERG waveform datasets in academic and clinical trial settings.

papers.title: Multidimensional sleep health and associated factors among community-dwelling Japanese adults: an age-stratified analysis.
papers.abstract: To investigate factors associated with multidimensional sleep health (MDSH), focusing on lifestyle factors, through a survey of community-dwelling Japanese adults. This cross-sectional study utilized a self-administered questionnaire survey conducted between December 2022 and February 2023 among Kyoto City residents aged 40 years or older. MDSH was assessed using the Ru-SATED scale, which evaluates six sleep health dimensions: regularity, satisfaction, alertness, timing, efficiency, and sleep duration. Lifestyle factors, including skipping breakfast, lack of exercise, alcohol consumption, current smoking, and higher body mass index (BMI ≥ 25), were examined. Associations between good sleep health (Ru-SATED score ≥ 10) and these factors were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression. An age-stratified analysis was conducted for participants younger than 75 years and those aged 75 years or older. Data from 661 respondents (57.9% female; mean age, 64.9 years) were included. The prevalence of good sleep health was 45.8% overall, 44.5% among those younger than 75 years, and 49.7% among those aged 75 years or older. Among all participants, older age and alcohol consumption were positively associated with good sleep health. Among participants younger than 75 years, exercise and alcohol consumption were positively associated with good sleep health. Among participants aged 75 years or older, a higher BMI (≥ 25) was negatively associated with good sleep health. Clarifying these age-specific factors associated with good sleep health provides valuable insights for developing tailored health initiatives in local communities with a focus on sleep health. Future studies are warranted to extend these findings in different populations.

papers.title: Non-coding RNAs in circadian network regulation and disease: from oscillatory coupling to precision chronomedicine.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are sustained by a hierarchically organized transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) that coordinates physiological processes across tissues. Emerging evidence indicates that non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and circular RNAs, are integral components of this oscillatory system. Rather than functioning solely as downstream regulators, ncRNAs modulate core clock genes, mediate environmental entrainment, and couple central and peripheral oscillators to tissue-specific outputs. Disruption of ncRNA-clock interactions destabilizes oscillatory amplitude, alters phase coherence, and weakens network robustness, thereby contributing to metabolic disorders, neuropsychiatric diseases, inflammatory conditions, and tumor progression. Increasing experimental evidence from inducible genetic models and functional rescue studies supports a causal role for specific ncRNAs in circadian network destabilization rather than mere association. Beyond local regulation, circulating and exosomal ncRNAs may act as systemic time signals that coordinate inter-organ communication. This systems-level perspective reframes circadian dysfunction as a network instability state in which feedback perturbations propagate across hierarchical clock layers. Future progress will require temporally resolved multi-omics approaches, tissue-specific perturbation models, and chronotherapeutic strategies aimed at restoring oscillatory amplitude and synchronization. Integrating ncRNA biology with circadian systems modeling may facilitate precision chronomedicine and help determine whether temporal architecture can serve as a modifiable therapeutic target.

papers.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

papers.title: Association of Newer Glucose-Lowering Medications and Phenoconversion From REM Sleep Behaviour Disorder to Parkinsonian Disorders in Older Adults with Type 2 Diabetes.
papers.abstract: It has been estimated that as many as 90% of patients with isolated REM behaviour disorder (iRBD) develop an α-synucleinopathy, yet there are currently no treatments proven to prevent or to delay phenoconversion. This study evaluated the association between glucose-lowering drug classes and incident Parkinson's disease (PD), parkinsonism, and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) among older adults with RBD and type 2 diabetes (T2D). We conducted a target trial emulation using a retrospective active-comparator new-user design with 2016-2020 Medicare fee-for-service claims data amongst beneficiaries ≥ 66 years with RBD and T2D and atleast 12 months of continuous enrollment before treatment initiation. We identified initators of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4is) or sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2is). Patients with prior use of either drug during the 12-month baseline period or initiation of both drugs on the index date were excluded. Hazard ratios for incident PD, parkinsonism or DLB were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models with stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting. Hazard ratios were estimated using Cox proportional regression models with inverse probability of treatment weighting. A total of 148, 144 and 138 patients were included in the GLP-1RA versus DPP-4i, GLP-1RA versus SGLT-2i and SGLT-2i versus DPP-4i cohorts, respectively. Compared with DPP-4i use, GLP-1RA use was associated with a lower risk of PD (HR, 0.02; 95% CI, 0.001-0.20), parkinsonism (HR, 0.08; 95% CI, 0.01-0.96) and the PD or parkinsonism composite (HR, 0.11; 95% CI, 0.01-0.83), but not DLB (HR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.04-5.37). Similarly, compared with DPP-4i use, SGLT-2i use was associated with a lower risk of PD (HR, 0.03; 95% CI, 0.001-0.97), parkinsonism (HR, 0.02; 95% CI, 0.001-0.87), and their composite (HR, 0.02; 95% CI, 0.001-0.86), but not DLB (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.17-5.17). No statistically significant differences were observed between GLP-1RA and SGLT-2i users. Amongst older adults with RBD and T2D, the risk of incident PD and parkinsonism differed by class of GLDs. Use of GLP-1RAs or SGLT-2is was associated with a lower risk of PD and parkinsonism compared with DPP-4is, while no significant differences were observed for DLB. No statistically significant differences were observed between GLP-1RAs and SGLT-2is. These findings warrant confirmation in studies with longer follow-up and larger sample sizes.

papers.title: From sleep associations to clinical event prediction: How can we make the next step?
Sleep in a warming world: Why heatwaves belong on the sleep medicine agenda.
Immediate transcranial magnetic stimulation-evoked potentials reveal short-latency intracortical inhibition.
papers.abstract: Short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) is the most widely used neurophysiological index of GABAergic inhibition in the human cortex. However, it is an indirect measure, inferring synaptic inhibition from suppression of peripherally recorded motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In the standard protocol, a subthreshold conditioning pulse suppresses the MEP evoked by a suprathreshold test pulse delivered 1-5 ms later. Interpretation is further complicated by temporal overlap with short-interval intracortical facilitation (SICF), reflecting excitatory interactions at interstimulus intervals of ∼1.5 and 2.7 ms. To overcome these limitations, we recorded immediate TMS-evoked EEG potentials (iTEPs; 1-10 ms post-stimulus) as a more direct measure of motor cortical activity in 16 healthy volunteers (20-35 years; seven male). The conventional SICI protocol suppressed only later components of the iTEP, probably corresponding to late corticospinal volleys previously identified in epidural spinal recordings after suprathreshold TMS, while the earliest iTEP component was unaffected. Importantly, later iTEPs were suppressed to a similar extent whether conditioning-test intervals coincided with SICF peaks or troughs, and the magnitude of iTEP suppression correlated with concurrently recorded paired-pulse MEP suppression. SICI also reduced an early TEP component (N15; 10-20 ms), but paired-pulse N15 suppression showed a different dependence on stimulus intensity and did not correlate with MEP suppression. These findings demonstrate that SICI measured via MEPs does not reflect a global index of cortical GABAergic motor cortical inhibition but instead reflects inhibition within specific cortical circuits that can be investigated more directly with iTEPs. KEY POINTS: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the primary motor cortex evokes high-frequency activity in the corticospinal tract, which can be measured directly with invasive, epidural recordings or indirectly as a time-locked, compound EMG response [i.e. motor evoked potential (MEP)]. GABAergic intracortical inhibition can be indexed as the MEP suppression caused by a subthreshold TMS pulse preceding the suprathreshold pulse by 1-5 ms. Combining TMS with artifact-minimized EEG allows the assessment of paired-pulse inhibition of immediate and early peaks of TMS-evoked EEG potential (TEP). Both immediate TEP (iTEP) and early TEP peaks display paired-pulse inhibition but only iTEP suppression relates to MEP suppression. iTEPs enable investigations of intracortical interactions non-invasively at the cortical level, which enables assessment of cortical and corticospinal physiology with TMS even in the absence of MEPs.

papers.title: Constraint-led thinking in the electrophysiology lab: a leadership reflection.
Spatiotemporal characterization of overdose mortality in Georgia, USA using spectral and nonlinear interaction analysis, 2003-2021.
papers.abstract: Drug overdose mortality in the United States exhibits strong geographic heterogeneity and complex temporal evolution, yet most spatiotemporal studies focus on trends and risks without explicitly characterizing the underlying dynamical structure of overdose trajectories. We develop a nonlinear spectral-spatiotemporal framework to analyze county-level overdose mortality in the state of Georgia from 2003 to 2021. Annual mortality rates are decomposed into low- and high-frequency components to distinguish long-term epidemic pressure from short-term variability, and nonlinear cross-frequency interaction is quantified using bispectral intensity. Counties are grouped into spectral phenotypes using unsupervised clustering. We find that overdose dynamics across Georgia are dominated by persistent low-frequency growth with limited independent short-term volatility. Nonlinear amplification is spatially concentrated and co-occurs with strong long-term epidemic pressure, and both features exhibit strong positive spatial autocorrelation across counties. Together, these results provide a mechanistically interpretable framework for identifying dynamical risk phenotypes and structural transitions in spatial overdose epidemics.

papers.title: School principals' burnout trajectories: Nature, predictors, and outcomes.
papers.abstract: This study seeks to achieve a dynamic person-centered understanding of the distinct burnout trajectories observed among 1574 Finnish school principals measured five times over a period of four years. Our results revealed that burnout trajectories corresponded to five main profiles: Low and Primarily Stable, Moderate and Primarily Stable, High and Increasing, Moderate and Increasing, and High and Stable. Perceptions of recognition, role clarity, role conflict, physical violence, and psychological violence were associated with these trajectories in a way that mainly supported our expectations. More precisely, initial levels (but not change in these levels) of these predictors were primary drivers of these trajectories, thereby reinforcing the importance of early intervention. Trajectories characterized by higher levels of burnout were also associated with lower levels of healthy lifestyle, sleep quality, work performance, and team efficacy, and with more difficulties regulating one's alcohol consumption and turnover intention. Conversely, trajectories characterized by lower levels of burnout were associated with better outcomes.

papers.title: Antipsychotic Use in Pediatric Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Trauma-Related Disorders.
papers.abstract: Childhood trauma is associated with a broad spectrum of psychiatric symptoms beyond core posttraumatic stress disorder criteria, including emotional dysregulation, aggression, sleep disturbance, and behavioral instability that impair functioning and safety. The pediatric evidence base is limited to case reports and small observational studies, with no randomized controlled trials. Adult data show modest and inconsistent benefits with notable adverse effects. Antipsychotics should be embedded within trauma-informed care, applied in a time-limited, symptom-specific manner, and closely monitored for metabolic, neurologic, and potential neurodevelopmental effects. Their role remains narrow and adjunctive, with psychotherapy, diagnostic precision, and risk minimization as primary priorities.
papers.journal: Child and adolescent psychiatric clinics of North America

papers.title: Antipsychotic Use in Adolescents with Substance Use and Substance Use Disorders.
papers.abstract: Antipsychotic medications are frequently prescribed off label in adolescents, particularly to manage agitation, behavioral dysregulation, and sleep disturbances, often in the context of substance use. However, their use is not consistently supported by a strong evidence base and carries meaningful risks, including metabolic, neurologic, and long-term health consequences. This article examines the clinical complexity of adolescents with substance use and co-occurring psychiatric symptoms, highlighting the risk of diagnostic ambiguity during acute intoxication or withdrawal. We provide a practical, developmentally informed framework to guide clinicians in the thoughtful, time-limited, and indication-specific use of antipsychotics in this population.
papers.journal: Child and adolescent psychiatric clinics of North America

papers.title: [Research on the underlying mechanisms of electroacupuncture in improving colonic dysmotility in ulcerative colitis mice based on cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channels].
papers.abstract: To study the mechanism of electroacupuncture (EA) of "Shangjuxu"(ST37) underlying improvement of colonic dysmotility in ulcerative colitis (UC) mice through regulating hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channel 2 (HCN2). Male C57BL/6J mice were randomized into control, model and EA groups, with 8 mice in each group. The UC model was established by giving 2.5% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) to the mice. EA (2 Hz/100 Hz, 0.9 mA) was applied at bilateral ST37 for 20 min, once a day for 7 d. The body weight, stool appearance and bloody stool conditions were recorded and the disease activity index (DAI) score was determined. The morphological changes of the colonic tissue were observed after H.E. staining. The changes of colonic motility before and after EA intervention were assessed by using in vivo and in vitro electrophysiological methods. The colonic transit time (glass bead method) and intestinal propulsion rate (ink mark method) were calculated. The positive expression of colonic HCN2, 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1), and serotonin transporter (SERT) were detected by immunofluorescence staining. The expression levels of TPH1 and SERT mRNAs and proteins were detected using real-time quantitative PCR and Western blot separately. The Vil1MerCreMerHCN2fl/fl mice were randomly divided into a control group and an induction group, with 8 mice in each group. The Vil1MerCreMerHCN2fl/fl mice were specifically conditionally knocked out the HCN2 gene in the intestinal epithelium. The mice in the induction group were injected with 5 mg/mL tamoxifen. ELISA was used to detect the contents of 5-HT and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) in the serum. The RIN-14B cells were divided into a normal group and a transfection group. The transfection group was knocked down the expression of HCN2 in the RIN-14B cells. ELISA was used to detect the contents of 5-HT and cAMP in the cell supernatants. Real-time quantitative PCR was used to detect the mRNA expressions of HCN2 and TPH1 in the RIN-14B cells. In contrast to the control group, the model group showed a significant decrease in the body weight and a notable increase in the DAI score and histopathological score (all P<0.001). In vivo and in vitro electrophysiology showed that DSS mice had significant colonic motility dysfunction, decreased frequency, amplitude, and the area under the curve (AUC) of colonic pressure curves (all P<0.001). Colonic transit time was strikingly prolonged while propulsion rate was significantly lower in DSS mice (all P<0.001). Expression of colonic HCN2, co-localized with 5-HT, were markedly increased (P<0.001), along with elevated expression of 5-HT, TPH1 and SERT (all P<0.001). All the increase and decrease of the indexes mentioned above were reversed by EA ( P<0.001, P<0.01, P<0.05). Conditional deletion of HCN2 in the intestinal epithelium markedly reduced the serum contents of 5-HT and cAMP ( P<0.001). Knockdown of HCN2 in RIN-14B cells reduced the expression levels of HCN2and TPH1 mRNAs (P<0.001), along with a significant decrease of the contents of 5-HT and cAMP in the cell supernatant (P<0.001). EA at ST37 can improve colonic dysmotility in UC mice by modulating the expression of HCN2 in enterochromaffin cells and regulating the release of 5-HT.

papers.title: Which elements of pulmonary rehabilitation improve physical activity and sleep in COPD? A systematic review and component network meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Physical activity (PA) predicts both mortality and morbidity. Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) is known to improve exercise capacity and quality of life, but it's impact on PA remains unclear. Likewise, it is uncertain which components of PR elicit the greatest response. To use component network meta-analysis (cNMA) to investigate the relative contribution of exercise modality and intensity, nonexercise components, type of supervision and programme duration of PR on PA and sleep behaviour for people with COPD. Medline, Embase, Cinahl and Cochrane databases were searched with no date or language restrictions. We included randomised controlled trials with an intervention involving exercise for people with COPD that measured PA or sleep behaviour as an outcome. A random-effects additive cNMA assessed the relative effectiveness of PR components on steps·day-1. Certainty of evidence was based on Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE). 50 studies (n=4136) reported a PA outcome and four studies reported a sleep outcome (n=638). The 34 studies measuring steps·day-1 were included in a cNMA (n=3039). PA increased following lower limb aerobic exercise (695 steps·day-1, 95% credible interval (CrI) 510-898; high certainty), strength training (390 steps·day-1, 95% CrI 63-811; low certainty), PA tracking (e.g. pedometers; 938 steps·day-1, 95% CrI 688-1480; low certainty). In-person supervised (-669 steps·day-1, 95% CrI -845--452; very low certainty) and remotely supervised (-685 steps·day-1, 95% CrI -1124--174; low certainty) programmes resulted in smaller changes in step count than unsupervised programmes. A meta-analysis of sleep outcomes was not possible due to the low number of studies reporting sleep as an outcome and heterogeneity in outcome measures used.
