[Clinical profile and management of patients with neuropathic pain treated with pregabalin in rehabilitation clinics in Spain: the PRELURE cross-sectional survey].
papers.abstract: To describe the clinical profile and management of patients with neuropathic pain referred for the first time to Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation clinics in Spain, as well as the use of pregabalin. A descriptive, nationwide survey based on aggregated data obtained through an online questionnaire. Each participant provided information on their last 6 patients with neuropathic pain referred for the first time and prescribed pregabalin at the consultation. A total of 124 specialists participated. Among their patients, chronic pain predominated (100.0%; Q1-Q3: 66.7-100.0), with a median duration of 8 months, as did mixed neuropathic-nociceptive pain (66.7%; Q1-Q3: 33.3-100.0). Baseline pain intensity (0-10) was high, with a mean score of 7.2 (SD 1.2) in women and 6.8 (SD 1.0) in men. Functional impairment, sleep and mood impairment were frequent. Before referral, pregabalin use was limited, with a mean initial dose of 104.9 (SD 65.7) mg/day in women and 130.5 (SD 110.8) mg/day in men. Following the consultation, the reported mean dose was 147.4 (SD 112.2) and 148.8 (SD 92.4) mg/day, respectively. Based on the physicians' retrospective estimates, at three months after treatmen adjustment, they perceived a reduction in the mean proportion of patients experiencing severe pain to 5.9% in women and 4.8% in men. Patients referred to Rehabilitation and treated with pregabalin present a high symptomatic and functional burden. Lower doses were observed before referral. After the consultation, treatment was adjusted and physicians perceived a reduction in patients with severe pain at three months.

papers.title: Melatonin, brain clearance, and dementia prevention: Revisiting the pineal-perivascular Axis.
papers.abstract: Melatonin has been proposed to support brain clearance of amyloid-β and tau, and its decline with age and in Alzheimer's disease has been interpreted as a contributor to clearance failure. The evidence underlying this proposal has not been appraised separately for endogenous pineal physiology and for administered melatonin. To review the evidence relating melatonin to perivascular transport and brain clearance, and to assess what that evidence can support. A critical narrative review. MEDLINE via PubMed, Scopus and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 31 August 2026, with an identical update search on 31 October 2026; database-specific strategies, dates, eligibility criteria and the selection process are reported in Section 3. Studies were appraised by what was manipulated (the organism's own pineal output, or administered melatonin at physiological or higher exposure, or actions not requiring receptor occupancy) and by the strength of design supporting each mechanistic claim. Animal doses were converted to human-equivalent doses by body-surface-area normalisation, with the method and its limitations stated in Section 3.6. The classification is applied in the tables; the text uses plain descriptions. In the literature identified, no study manipulated endogenous pineal melatonin while measuring perivascular transport or clearance, and no study combined a melatonin receptor antagonist or receptor deletion with a clearance readout. A causal role for endogenous melatonin therefore remains untested. Positive preclinical findings used administered melatonin at exposures estimated to be two to four orders of magnitude above standard clinical dosing on a body-weight basis, and approximately 40 to 900 times standard dosing after body-surface-area normalisation, which limits their extension to routine supplementation. The timing of melatonin secretion relative to sleep-associated clearance differs between nocturnal rodents and diurnal humans, which constrains translation from rodent models. Human data are limited by the absence of a validated non-invasive measure of brain clearance. Available evidence is consistent with pharmacological modulation of components of the clearance system. Whether endogenous pineal melatonin regulates brain clearance has not been tested. Pinealectomy with timed replacement in a melatonin-proficient animal, and the addition of a receptor antagonist arm to existing designs, would address the principal gaps.

papers.title: Unhealthy lifestyle profiles and the risk of incident depressive symptoms: Findings from the French CONSTANCES population-based cohort.
papers.abstract: The link between unhealthy lifestyle factors and incident depressive symptoms is well evidenced but less is known about how lifestyle profiles relate to this risk. Analyses were conducted on 23,711 participants recruited from the general population French CONSTANCES cohort before 2015 and free of baseline depressive symptoms (DepS) (mean age: 49.0 (SD 12.9), 49.6% men). DepS was assessed using the CES-D scale (score ≥ 16) at baseline and at three follow-ups. Latent class analysis was performed on baseline lifestyle factors (diet, physical activity, body mass index, sleep duration, alcohol consumption, smoking, cannabis use). Longitudinal associations with incident DepS were analysed using Cox proportional hazard models. The selected latent class model identified five lifestyle profiles: an 'Overall healthy' profile (36.4% of the sample, age and sex-adjusted incidence rate (95% CI): 66.8 (57.2-78.1)), 'Healthy active ex-smoker' profile (26.9%, 61.5 (50.2-75.4)), 'Moderately healthy, overweight and drinking' profile (15%, 43.8 (26.4-72.8)), 'Unhealthy, drinking and smoking' profile (11%, 55.8 (43.6-71.5) and 'Overall unhealthy' profile (10.7%, 86.7 (62.6-120.2)). In the fully-adjusted model, compared to the 'Overall healthy' profile, the greatest increase in DepS risk was observed for the 'Overall unhealthy' profile (HR (95% CI): 1.25 (1.15-1.35)), followed by the younger physically active 'Unhealthy, drinking and smoking' profile (1.17 (1.08-1.27)). Our findings highlight an increased incident DepS risk for the two unhealthiest profiles, with a distinct at-risk younger physically active drinking and smoking profile. In addition to considering individual lifestyle factors, targeting distinct high-risk profiles may prove useful for tailoring future interventions.

papers.title: Night shift work and subclinical cardiac remodelling: a multi-omic CMR study in 42 671 individuals.
papers.abstract: Whether frequent night-shift work is associated with a distinct subclinical cardiac phenotype and accompanying molecular alterations remains uncertain. We analysed 42 671 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease who underwent cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). Night-shift frequency was classified into four categories, and 15 CMR measures were assessed using multivariable regression. Compared with day workers, frequent night-shift workers showed greater left ventricular global wall thickness [standardized β = 0.092, 95% CI 0.050-0.135; false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.001] and left ventricular mass-to-volume ratio (β = 0.072, 95% CI 0.021-0.123; FDR = 0.019), with lower left ventricular end-diastolic volume index, right ventricular end-diastolic volume index, right ventricular stroke volume index, and maximal right atrial volume index (all FDR < 0.05). Left ventricular global circumferential strain was less favourable (β = 0.092, 95% CI 0.040-0.144; FDR = 0.002), whereas left ventricular ejection fraction and global longitudinal strain were not significantly associated. Proteomic (n = 4889) and metabolomic (n = 42 671) analyses identified exploratory inflammatory, vascular, and lipid-related correlates. Mediation analyses identified FDR-significant indirect-effect estimates involving left ventricular end-diastolic volume index for three proteins and four metabolites. Two-sample Mendelian randomization identified associations between selected molecular features and CMR traits, although directions were not uniformly concordant with the observational estimates. Frequent night shift work was associated with greater concentric left ventricular geometry, lower cardiac chamber volumes, and less favourable circumferential strain, together with inflammatory and lipid-related molecular correlates. Prospective studies are required to determine temporal relationships and long-term clinical relevance.

papers.title: Postoperative Sleep Quality in Children: Development and Psychometric Evaluation of a Questionnaire.
papers.abstract: Sleep in the immediate postoperative period is influenced by multiple perioperative factors. A key limitation in current research and clinical practice is the lack of brief, psychometrically robust instruments specifically designed to assess postoperative sleep. The aim of this study is to evaluate the psychometric properties of a short questionnaire assessing postoperative sleep quality in children and adolescents. The questionnaire was developed based on a literature review and 48 semi-structured interviews. This is a retrospective analysis. Out of 685 postoperative paediatric patients included across three studies (Study 1: n = 120; age: 14.7 ± 1.9 years, female: 43%; Study 2: n = 249; age: median 5.5, IQR: 4.5-6.5, female: 44%; Study 3: n = 312; age: median 12.0, IQR: 9.3-14.0, female: 38%), 88.5% (n = 609) could be included in the final analysis. Item response theory analysis was used to analyse factorial structure, reliability and measurement invariance (differential item functioning-DIF). A two-factor structure was identified: F1: Pain related impaired sleep quality and F2: General sleep quality with three items loading high on each factor could be identified (RMSEA: 0.01, 90% CI: < 0.01 to 0.06; CFI: 0.997, TLI: 0.996). Reliability was good (< 0.8) for relevant sleep quality ranges. No relevant DIF was observed with respect to sex or response mode. The Post-operative Sleep Questionnaire for children (Po-S-C) is a new short questionnaire for assessing postoperative sleep quality in children and adolescents showing good reliability and no measurement invariance. Further studies are needed to replicate these results in other samples.

papers.title: Rapid prey capture learning slowly resets activity set points in rat binocular visual cortex.
papers.abstract: Neurons within primary visual cortex (V1) possess stable firing rate set points to which they faithfully return when perturbed by passive sensory manipulations. Chronic recordings in vivo suggest that these set points are present early in postnatal development and are stable through adulthood, raising the possibility that once they are established, they are largely immutable. Here, we challenge this idea using an ethological, vision-dependent prey capture learning paradigm in juvenile rats. Juvenile rats rapidly (in 1 day) became proficient at catching crickets. This learning was impaired when V1 was inactivated and was accompanied by an increase in the number of binocular V1 (V1b) neurons with firing reliably tied to specific behavioral epochs during hunts, indicating that hunting drives rapid functional plasticity within V1b. Remarkably, this rapid learning set in motion a slow, state-dependent increase in V1b firing that began after learning was complete and persisted for days. This upward firing rate plasticity was gradual, occurred selectively during wake states, and in L2/3 was driven by a TNF-α-dependent increase in excitatory synaptic drive onto pyramidal neurons-all features of homeostatic forms of V1 plasticity. Finally, TNF-α inhibition administered after learning was complete prevented this change in network excitability and impaired the consolidation of hunting skills. Taken together, these data suggest that naturalistic learning co-opts homeostatic forms of plasticity to reset firing rate setpoints within V1b, in a process that facilitates consolidation of learning.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnea and lung cancer risk: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: This relationship between obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and lung malignancy has been reported previously, but remains controversial. The aim of this systematic review is to evaluate the hypothesis that OSAs is a potential hazard for the development of lung cancer. We performed a structured review in PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase and Web of Science databases from inception through September 2024 to yield the data underlying a comparison of lung cancer risk in individuals with and without OSA. Aggregated hazard ratios (HRs) along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were determined utilizing random-effects statistical models. The systematic review included eight cohort studies. Of these, 7 studies with adjusted HR and RR were included in the meta analysis ( N = 7,641,402), which showed robust association with higher lung Cancer incidence (HR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.03-1.49), and higher risk in studies with a six to nine-year followup (HR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.27-1.38). Findings were generally robust having been supported by sensitivity analysis. There was a lack of robust power of the publication-bias tests as the number of studies in the analyses was low ( P = 0.744 for Egger's test). Six studies that used a retrospective group design showed similar patterns (HR = 1.21, 95% CI: 0.99-1.47). OSA is associated with an elevated risk for cancer of the lungs, particularly during mid-term follow-up (6-9 years). The large standard deviation emphasises the need for a standardised procedure for the implementation of OSA screening and covariate adjustments in follow-up trials.

papers.title: Deciphering mitochondrial dysfunction and circadian rhythm-related pathogenic patterns for the pathogenesis of Kawasaki Disease and corresponding nursing therapeutic enrichment: Evidence from machine learning-driven multi-omics and clinical validation.
papers.abstract: Kawasaki Disease (KD) is an acute, self-limited vasculitis of childhood, with its etiopathogenesis intricately tied to systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Disruption of circadian rhythms and mitochondrial transport, 2 fundamental homeostatic systems, are increasingly recognized as independent contributors to vascular pathology. However, their integrated molecular crosstalk in KD remains completely uncharted. The primary objective was to identify and validate a mitochondrial transport andcircadian rhythm (MRC)-related molecular signature in KD. The secondary objectives were to resolve MRC-defined molecular subtypes, to nominate and characterize a candidate hub gene, to define its cellular distribution, and to prioritize candidate therapeutic compounds. First, Peripheral blood bulk transcriptomic datasets of KD patients were analyzed. GSE68004 was interrogated via Limma, GSVA, and WGCNA to isolate MRC-associated shared DEGs. Second, non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and 3 machine learning algorithms (RF, Lasso and SVM-RFE) were deployed in GSE63881 for molecular subtype identification and diagnostic model construction, with independent diagnostic validation in integrated GSE73463 and GSE73462. Next, leveraging single-cell transcriptomic data from peripheral blood samples of KD patients (GSE24757), we resolved the spatiotemporal dissemination and functional evolution of the hub gene. In addition, deep learning-driven drug screening (DrugReflector) and molecular docking nominated a candidate compound in GSE18606. Finally, differential expression of the hub gene was validated using q-RT-PCR in clinical samples from KD patients. The integrated MRC-related signature robustly stratified KD patients into 2 distinct molecular subgroups. FNDC5 was identified as an NK-distributed and MRC-related pathogenic factor in KD. BRD-K10482608 was nominated as a computationally predicted candidate targeting FNDC5 for KD. This study provides the first pathway-anchored MRC-related signature in KD together with a validated framework for molecular stratification. FNDC5 is put forward as a prioritized, hypothesis-generating candidate of KD vasculopathy, and BRD-K10482608 as a computationally nominated starting point for future functional and nursing pharmacological testing.

papers.title: Hybrid framework utilizing interval Type-2 fuzzy entropy and ScaleDual-CNN for differential diagnosis of dementia using rest-state EEG signals.
papers.abstract: Differential diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is challenging because of their similarity in early stages. Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals offer a non-invasive, inexpensive tool for automated screening. However, traditional approaches cannot handle environmental noise and high inter-individual variance. In this study, interval type-2 fuzzy entropy (IT2-FE) was evaluated as a biomarker for diagnosing dementia under uncertainty. We utilized the public OpenNeuro ds004504 database (88 resting-state subjects). Signals were segmented into 4-s windows. Then we extracted IT2-FE in the alpha and theta bands, Hjorth and connectivity features. A dual evaluation framework was developed. First, we evaluated a subject-independent pipeline by combining fuzzy features, deep network, and SVM classifier. Second, we implemented an epoch-based model by combining the customized ScaleDual-CNN with fuzzy/spectral features and the XGBoost classifier. Compared to spectral entropy, the IT2-FE method identified approximately 11.7 times more statistically significant features (35 versus 3; pFDR < 0.05). These findings indicate statistically significant differences between the groups. For entropy-based classification, IT2-FE achieved 67.64% accuracy and 61.72% macro-F1, compared with 62.50% and 60.55% for spectral entropy, and 62.50% and 60.01% for Type-1 fuzzy entropy, respectively. These results suggest that IT2-FE captures discriminative EEG characteristics, although its classification performance advantage over other entropy measures remains limited. Subject-independent AUC for control, AD, and FTD were 0.96, 0.93, and 0.89, respectively. Epoch-level accuracy and F1 scores reached 95.29% and 94.85%. Ablation analysis demonstrated that combining deep embeddings with IT2-FE features improved classification performance. The proposed framework holds promise for computer-aided dementia diagnosis.

papers.title: The minimum temporal derivative of the unipolar electrogram downslope as a measure of local 3D conduction velocity in arrhythmogenic myocardium.
papers.abstract: Re-entrant arrhythmias may be non-inducible or haemodynamically poorly tolerated, requiring substrate mapping to assess myocardial electrophysiological properties. Abnormally slowly conducting tissue, deemed critical to the initiation and maintenance of re-entrant circuits, serves as a potential catheter ablation target. However, obtaining in-procedure local conduction velocity (CV) measurements remains challenging. A more robust approach for determining local CV may enhance accurate ablation target identification. We sought to determine whether the minimum temporal derivative of the unipolar electrogram downslope voltage, [Formula: see text] , provides a novel quantitative measure of local 3D myocardial CV, presenting a unique parameter for identifying arrhythmogenic tissue. Bidomain simulations with a realistic computational ventricular slab model were performed to establish the impact of altering sodium channel conductance, gap junction conductivity, fibrosis density, fibrosis depth, tissue thickness and electrode size on unipolar electrogram metrics. Furthermore, [Formula: see text] was correlated with local CV during sodium channel block, gap junction inhibition, and ischemia, with findings corroborated in a computational human ventricular model. In computational simulations, increasing fibrosis density or reducing sodium channel conductance and gap junction conductivity slowed CV, producing a corresponding inverse linear correlation between [Formula: see text] and 2D surface-based and 3D volume-based CV. During non-planar stimulation with a transmural component, a similar relationship was identified between [Formula: see text] and 3D CV. Findings were additionally supported by quantitatively comparable trends in a computational human ventricular model. The study indicates that [Formula: see text] is directly correlated with local 3D CV, and may have utility in substrate mapping of non-inducible or haemodynamically compromising arrhythmias and intra-procedural in-silico model parameterisation.

papers.title: Beyond sensitivity: Performance, methodological heterogeneity, and real-time translation of wrist-worn convulsive seizure detection devices - A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Wrist-worn seizure-detection devices can detect convulsive seizures, but pooled performance estimates may obscure methodological differences between studies. We evaluated the performance, heterogeneity, and translational readiness of wrist-worn non-EEG systems for automated detection of convulsive and generalized tonic-clonic (GTC) seizures. We systematically searched MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Event-level sensitivity for convulsive and GTC seizures was pooled using random-effects generalized linear mixed models; false-alarm rates (FARs) were pooled as incidence rates per 24 h. We evaluated heterogeneity, prespecified subgroups, methodological variability, detection latency, and progression to real-time intervention. Twenty studies comprising 1598 participants and 71,310 monitoring hours were included. Pooled random-effects sensitivity was approximately 93% for convulsive seizures and 96% for GTC seizures, with heterogeneity exceeding 75% for both outcomes. The pooled FAR was approximately 0.39/24 h, with heterogeneity approaching 99%. Neither sensing modality, study phase, population, algorithm locking, nor offline versus real-time processing explained performance differences under random-effects modeling. Methodological variability extended to seizure eligibility, amplitude and duration thresholds, temporal windowing, classifier architecture, operating-point selection, validation strategy, and FAR denominator construction. Mean detection latency was 30.04 s across nine reporting studies. Only one study directly evaluated translation from detection to real-time caregiver notification and intervention. Wrist-worn devices demonstrate high sensitivity for convulsive and GTC seizure detection, but performance is not yet methodologically uniform or consistently generalizable. Standardized evaluation and independent validation are needed, with future studies extending beyond detection accuracy to reliable real-time alert delivery and actionable intervention.

papers.title: Intranasal dexmedetomidine sedation in pediatric electroencephalography: dose optimization, safety, and EEG characteristics.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intranasal dexmedetomidine (DEX) for sedation during pediatric EEG and to explore whether EEG spectral characteristics under DEX differ from those under chloral hydrate. In this retrospective cohort study, 224 children (0-18 years) who underwent EEG under intranasal DEX sedation at a single tertiary center (January 2024-April 2025) were analyzed. Patients were stratified into weight-based dosing (Group 1, <50 kg; median 2 μg/kg) and fixed dosing (Group 2, ≥50 kg; median 100 μg). Sedation success, onset time, total sedation time, and adverse events were assessed. In a within-subject subgroup of 11 patients with a prior chloral hydrate EEG, relative power spectral density (rPSD) in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands during N1 and N2 sleep was compared using patient-level paired analyses, with mean paired differences, 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and correction for multiple comparisons. Initial sedation success was 94.6% in Group 1 and 94.7% in Group 2; all patients achieved adequate sedation after rescue dosing. Median onset time was 10 minutes in both groups. Adverse events were mild and self-limited (3.2% and 2.6%). No statistically significant differences in rPSD between DEX and chloral hydrate were detected in either sleep stage after correction for multiple comparisons; however, the CIs were wide, and equivalence could not be established. Interictal epileptiform discharges were visually unchanged. Intranasal DEX is an effective, well-tolerated sedative for pediatric EEG, and a weight-stratified dosing strategy appears practical. In a small paired subgroup, no significant spectral differences from chloral hydrate were detected; these preliminary quantitative findings warrant confirmation in larger studies.

papers.title: Psychological Impact of Severe Intraoperative Complications on Surgeons: A Multicenter Study.
papers.abstract: Severe intraoperative complications may cause death or long-term morbidity. Although patient consequences are recognized, the psychological burden on surgeons remains insufficiently addressed. Surgeons involved in adverse events may become "second victims," experiencing distress that can affect their well-being, professional confidence, decision-making, and subsequent practice. This study aimed to evaluate surgeons' psychological responses following severe intraoperative complications, describe coping and support-seeking behaviors, assess changes in surgical practice, and examine perceptions of institutional psychological support. A multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted among surgeons using an anonymous questionnaire developed in French and English. The questionnaire was distributed via e-mail and WhatsApp to surgeons working across a hospital network in Lebanon. It assessed professional characteristics, exposure to severe intraoperative complications, emotional responses, coping and support-seeking behaviors, debriefing experiences, changes in practice, and perceptions of institutional support. Data were exported to Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Descriptive analyses were performed, and an exploratory ten-item Emotions score was assessed for internal consistency using Cronbach's alpha. Its association with age was explored using Pearson correlation. Sixty-nine surgeons participated, and 51 (73.9%) reported at least one severe intraoperative complication. Stress and anxiety were reported at moderate or higher levels by 94.1% and 90.2% of exposed surgeons, respectively. Sleep disturbance affected 68.6%, and 56.9% feared damage to their professional reputation. The exploratory Emotions score demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.91). In an exploratory analysis, older age was modestly associated with a lower Emotions score (r = -0.305; P = 0.029). More than half sought no professional or personal support, 62.7% participated in no debriefing, and 92.2% considered institutional psychological support insufficient. Severe intraoperative complications are associated with psychological distress among surgeons, yet structured support remains uncommon. Confidential peer support, systematic debriefing, mentorship, stress-management training, and psychological care should be integrated into quality-improvement and patient-safety strategies.

papers.title: The insular cortex and arousal: insights from a human focal lesion-based model.
papers.abstract: Wakefulness depends on distributed cortico-subcortical networks integrating arousal and cognitive processes. Although the insular cortex is not traditionally considered a core component of sleep-wake regulation, its connectivity suggests a modulatory role in humans. We retrospectively investigated patients with insular gliomas undergoing awake craniotomy with intraoperative neurophysiological and neuropsychological monitoring. We identified patients exhibiting transient episodes of impaired task engagement and responsiveness during active intraoperative testing, defined as the intra-surgical falling asleep phenomenon (ISFAP) based primarily on behavioral and task-related criteria. Associated electroencephalographic (EEG) and electrocorticographic (ECoG) features were subsequently characterized as supportive neurophysiological correlates. These patients were compared with matched controls who did not develop ISFAP. Forty-six patients were included (22 ISFAP; 24 controls). ISFAP was associated with neurophysiological patterns resembling non-rapid eye movement sleep, including theta-delta slow waves and spindle-like oscillatory activity. In univariate analyses, ISFAP was more frequent in right-sided insular tumors and patients receiving train-of-five stimulation, although these associations were not retained in multivariable models. Within the ISFAP group, inability to resume task performance after episode onset was associated with left-sided lesions. ISFAP is a transient behavioral phenomenon accompanied by sleep-like neurophysiological features during cognitive engagement in a subset of patients undergoing awake surgery for insular gliomas. These findings raise the hypothesis of transient arousal instability in the context of lesion-related network dysfunction, potentially influenced by the awake-surgery setting. Recognition of ISFAP may improve the interpretation of neuropsychological performance during awake surgery.

papers.title: Ayurvedic management of mixed-type obsessive-compulsive disorder along with comorbid depression (Atatvabhinivesha): A case report.
papers.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic and debilitating neuropsychiatric condition characterised by persistent intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviours performed to alleviate anxiety or distress. Ayurveda describes a similar entity, Atatvabhinivesha, a Manovikara characterised by delusional adherence to false beliefs due to Rajo-tamo vitiation. A 34-year-old male, pre-diagnosed with mixed type OCD with comorbid depression, presented to Ayurvedic hospital with obsessive cleaning rituals, intrusive thoughts, disturbed sleep with hypnic jerks, and sustained anxiety for two years. Despite two months of conventional treatment, symptom control remained inadequate. The patient was managed through Panchakarma [Virechana Karma (∼purgation therapy), Basti Karma (∼enema therapy), Nasya Karma (∼nasal drops therapy)] followed by oral Medhya Rasayana for 45 days of IPD. Oral Medhya Rasayana was prescribed with Pathya-apathya for the next 5 months in OPD. Daivavyapashraya chikitsa [Gayatri Mantra chanting, Havan, meditation, Moti Dharana, etc.] was also performed throughout the treatment. Marked reduction in HAM-D (26 to 5), Y-BOCS (28 to 6) scores, and almost complete relief in symptoms were observed. The quality of life of the patient was also improved. The conventional medicine dosage was reduced in a tapering dose up to 3 months and was completely stopped by the patient after 3 months of Ayurvedic treatment without any symptomatic aggravation. Even after 1 year from the date of admission, no relapse was observed, despite discontinuation of all oral medications for the past six months. This case highlights the efficacy of Ayurvedic treatment in OCD comorbid with depression management without any clinically apparent or patient-reported adverse effects during the treatment period.

papers.title: In-vivo acute oral toxicity of Munzij and Mushile Balgham Advia decoctions used in Unani Medicine.
papers.abstract: In Unani Medicine, Joshanda (decoction) of Munzij and Mushil-e-Balgham drugs is traditionally used for disorders associated with Sue Mizaj Balghami (imbalance of phlegmatic humour), including Falij (hemiplegia), Istirkha (flaccidity), Khadar (numbness), and Rasha (tremor). Despite clinical evidence of its therapeutic efficacy, its toxicity profile remains unexplored. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate its acute oral toxicity following OECD Guideline 423. To evaluate the acute oral toxicity of traditionally used Munzij and Mushil-e-Balgham decoctions to support their historical safety profile. Female Wistar rats were divided into four groups (n = 6, three rats per step); Group I (control) received distilled water, while Groups II, III, and IV received 2000 mg/kg of aqueous extracts of Munzij, Mushil, and Munzij + Mushil drugs, respectively, orally. Rats were observed individually for various toxic signs for 14 days, with close monitoring during the initial hours. Special attention was given to tremors, convulsions, salivation, diarrhoea, lethargy, sleep, coma, and mortality. The weights of the animals, water consumption, and food intake were weekly recorded. At the end, animals were euthanized, and external and internal necropsies were performed. Relative organ weight was calculated. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS version 28.0.0.0 software. No significant changes were observed in Irwin test parameters, body weight, food and water intake, necropsy findings, relative organ weights, or mortality in any test group compared to control group. The study showed no mortality or morbidity at the limit dose of 2000 mg/kg, considering their long history of traditional use without reported adverse effects.

papers.title: Nocturnal Respiratory Rate and Variability Predict Long-Term Mortality in Stable Outpatients With Cardiovascular Risk Factors.
papers.abstract: Respiratory rate predicts short-term mortality in acute care settings, yet its prognostic significance in clinically stable outpatients remains poorly defined. The objective of the study was to determine whether the median and variability of nocturnal respiratory rate (NRR) are independently associated with long-term cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in outpatients with cardiovascular risk factors. We analyzed overnight chest belt waveforms from elective polysomnography in 5,679 adults with cardiovascular risk enrolled in the Sleep Heart Health Study. NRR was quantified at 30-second resolution, and per-subject median NRR and within-night variability (interdecile range) were derived. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations with cardiovascular and all-cause mortality over 3-year and 15-year follow-up periods, adjusting for demographic characteristics, cardiopulmonary comorbidities, and sleep apnea severity. Higher median NRR and greater interdecile range of NRR were each associated with increased cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. Combining these metrics stratified participants into low-, mid-, and high-risk groups with graded 3-year all-cause mortality; relative to the low-risk group, mortality risk increased stepwise in the mid-risk group (unadjusted HR: 1.91; 95% CI: 1.39-2.64; P < 0.001; adjusted HR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.09-2.10; P = 0.012) and the high-risk group (unadjusted HR: 4.17; 95% CI: 2.85-6.10; P < 0.001; adjusted HR: 2.80; 95% CI: 1.88-4.15; P < 0.001). Both the baseline level and variability of NRR independently predict mortality in clinically stable adults with cardiovascular risk. Densely profiled NRR represents a promising, underutilized biomarker for long-term risk stratification.

papers.title: Preferential responses to spectrally degraded sentences in the human cortex revealed by intracranial electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: Despite progress in cochlear implant (CI) technology, there is considerable variability in outcomes, in part attributed to the function of central auditory pathways. Spectrally degraded sounds presented to normal-hearing listeners can be used to approximate cortical sound processing by CI users. Prior intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) work identified "clear-preferred" and less common "vocoded-preferred" differential responses to clear and noise-vocoded non-word speech tokens. Better identification of vocoded consonants was associated with activation of the cortical dorsal auditory stream. The present study further characterized these differential responses using sentence stimuli that are expected to engage the ventral processing stream. Participants were neurosurgical epilepsy patients undergoing iEEG monitoring. Sentences were degraded using a 3-band noise vocoder. Analysis of iEEG data focused on event-related band power (ERBP) between 4-150 Hz. Differential responses (ERBP augmentation or suppression) to clear and vocoded sentences were observed both in early and late portions of the sentence, suggesting a sustained, rather than transient, nature of the preferential responses. Clear-preferred responses are likely driven by spectral complexity and intelligibility. Vocoded-preferred responses may reflect increased processing demands associated with challenging listening conditions. These responses occurred primarily in core auditory cortex and regions along the dorsal auditory stream but were virtually absent in prefrontal cortex. Identifying regions involved in the processing of degraded speech has potential clinical utility and may present candidate targets for neuromodulation-based CI rehabilitation strategies.

papers.title: A state-of-the-art review of biosensor-based markers for tinnitus.
papers.abstract: This review critically evaluates biosensor-based approaches for identifying objective biosensor-based markers of tinnitus, emphasising multimodal integration and clinical translation. Ovid Medline, Embase, and PubMed were searched from 2004 to 2026. The search strategy used the keywords "tinnitus" and names of techniques, including electroencephalogram (EEG), magnetoencephalography (MEG), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electrocardiogram (ECG), Galvanic skin response (GSR), sleep actigraphy, and event-related potential (ERP). Synonym expansion was used to include more pertinent search terms from the identified papers. The results of the review were catalogued and organised into themes by technique and analysis method. This literature review identified electrophysiological techniques, brain imaging, and physiological features that may provide objective evidence of tinnitus. Findings for each method are presented and compared. Several candidate markers indicate increased association among the auditory cortex, thalamus, and limbic system. EEG appears to be a promising and practical approach to developing objective measures of tinnitus. However, inconsistent findings and poor reproducibility currently limit its clinical application. Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods to distinguish between tinnitus sufferers and non-sufferers using biosensor data are promising. While numerous biosensor-based marker candidates for tinnitus have been proposed, variability and poor reproducibility remain major barriers. This is a rapidly developing field. Until results are robust and replicable, claims that an effective marker for tinnitus has been identified should be considered with caution.

papers.title: EEG-based depression detection via temporal-frequency-dynamical feature fusion.
papers.abstract: Depression has become a major global mental health illness. Electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression detection, combined with machine learning techniques, provides a promising route for developing novel diagnostic or screening measures. Most existing works represent complex EEG signals using domain-specific information, ignoring the complementarity among the temporal, frequency, and nonlinear dynamical characteristics. This hinders their ability to comprehensively capture the dynamic variations of EEG, thereby restricting model performance. To address this problem, the current work proposes a sorting-guided multi-domain feature coupling framework for depression detection. Specifically, the proposed method extracts meaningful features from the temporal, frequency, and nonlinear dynamical perspectives to characterize EEG signals. Then, an ordered feature coupling strategy is introduced to interactively fuse multi-view characteristics, thereby yielding a better yet compact feature representation. The resulting features can be effectively classified using standard machine learning classifiers. The proposed framework is evaluated on two datasets for distinct classification tasks: discriminating patients with major depressive disorder from healthy controls using MODMA database and distinguishing questionnaire-defined high-risk from low-risk individuals for depression using EDRA database. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the presented approach. This study provides a novel perspective on distinguishing different types of EEG signals, laying the groundwork for future research.

papers.title: Spider Pattern: An adaptive EEG feature extraction method for Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia classification.
papers.abstract: Dementia is a major and growing health challenge, and electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive and comparatively accessible modality for computational investigation of dementia-related brain activity. This study evaluates an adaptive time-domain feature extraction technique named Spider Pattern (SP), combined with Social Spider Algorithm (SSA) feature selection and feedforward neural network (FFNN) classification, for Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and normal control (NC) discrimination. The preprocessed public EEG dataset contains 88 participants (36 AD, 23 FTD, and 29 NC). Using 15-second non-overlapping segmentation, 4535 segments were analyzed and represented by 608 SP features. The primary evaluation used nested leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation in which SSA feature selection was performed only within each outer training fold. Subject-level accuracies were 78.46% for AD vs. NC (AUC 0.810), 71.15% for FTD vs. NC (AUC 0.712), and 52.54% for AD vs. FTD (AUC 0.562). Exact paired McNemar tests showed no significant difference between SSA and either full-feature or mRMR comparators. A secondary segment-wise 10-fold analysis using all 608 SP features produced higher accuracies of 90.83%, 93.08%, and 90.87%, respectively; however, every fold contained test participants also represented in training, so these values are not estimates of unseen-subject generalization. The gap between the two estimates quantifies the effect of participant leakage on this widely used public dataset. Sensitivity analyses showed task-dependent effects of SP design choices, while repeated SSA runs showed limited feature-subset stability. The results support further investigation of SP for case-control EEG classification but do not establish reliable AD-vs.-FTD discrimination or clinical deployment.

papers.title: Disease severity and treatment associations in narcolepsy type 1: a real-world long-term prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: The long-term disease severity of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) under routine treatment is insufficiently characterised. In a real-world setting, we examined disease severity changes from unmedicated baseline to medicated follow-up in a large NT1 cohort. We assessed 130 children and adults with NT1 twice (unmedicated baseline; follow-up under routine treatment (92.3% medicated); mean 5.5 years apart). Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Stanford Sleep Questionnaire, polysomnography, multiple sleep latency test (MSLT), and BMI were assessed. Baseline and follow-up were compared, stratified by ± sodium oxybate use. Additionally, adjusted regression models examined associations between disease severity and age, sex, disease duration, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) hypocretin-1, and medication categories (wake-promoting, antidepressants, sodium oxybate), including sex/age-by-medication interactions. From baseline to follow-up, ESS, REM-related symptom frequency and number of sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs) decreased; MSLT mean sleep latency (MSL) increased (all p < 0.01). Nocturnal sleep fragmentation and adult BMI increased only in sodium oxybate non-users. In regression models, baseline severity significantly predicted follow-up severity for nearly all corresponding outcomes and at both timepoints, female sex was persistently associated with higher ESS and more frequent cataplexy, younger age with more MSLT SOREMPs, and undetectable hypocretin-1 (<40 pg/ml) with shorter MSL. Further, the association between sodium oxybate and MSL differed by sex. In a real-world setting, overall NT1 disease severity improved from unmedicated baseline to medicated follow-up, with most favourable trajectories in sodium oxybate users. Despite medication, baseline severity predicted follow-up severity, and female sex, younger age, and undetectable CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency were associated with greater severity at both timepoints. Our findings highlight that substantial improvements under routine treatment coexist with long-term persistent differences in disease severity. This underlines heterogeneity of NT1 trajectories and the importance of considering treatment as well as sex, age, and hypocretin deficiency in the long-term clinical management of NT1.

papers.title: Rest-to-task transfer of sparse-to-full EEG reconstruction for cognitive-load decoding.
papers.abstract: Sparse-to-full electroencephalography (EEG) reconstruction holds great promise for reducing electrode burden while maintaining compatibility with multichannel analysis pipelines. This study examined whether a convolutional neural network trained exclusively on resting-state EEG could preserve task-relevant information when transferred to previously unseen N-back working memory tasks without task-specific fine-tuning.Approach. A 4-to-21-channel reconstruction model was evaluated using four different sparse electrode configurations (CROSS, DSI, EMOT, MUSE) in participants with major depressive disorder, who served as a clinically heterogeneous test cohort rather than a disorder-specific classification target. Reconstruction was comprehensively assessed based on complementary signal-level metrics, the preservation of both overall power spectral density and workload-related spectral contrasts, and within-subject cognitive-load classification across task-repetition groups.Main results. The preferred electrode configuration depended on the evaluation endpoint. In generic waveform reconstruction, EMOT had the best composite rank for generic reconstruction fidelity and a tie-adjusted winner frequency of 61.4%, although it did not lead all individual metrics. In contrast, CROSS showed the strongest preservation of overall spectral structure and 2-back versus 0-back spectral contrast and had the highest binary classification performance among the reconstructed configurations. However, the relationship between generic reconstruction fidelity and spectral preservation reversed from positive in pooled analysis to negative within participants, and spectral preservation was not significantly associated with binary classification accuracy at the participant level.Significance. These results demonstrate that resting-state-trained sparse-to-full EEG reconstruction can partially preserve task-related spectral representation without task-specific fine-tuning. However, our findings reveal a critical caveat: high-fidelity waveform-level reconstruction does not necessarily correspond to superior preservation of cognitive-task features. Ultimately, these findings show that reconstruction quality is endpoint dependent, underscoring the necessity of a multidimensional validation combining generic signal fidelity, task-specific spectral preservation, and downstream model behavior.
