papers.title: Passive Monitoring for Detecting Hypomanic Symptoms in Bipolar Disorder Using Explainable Machine Learning: Longitudinal Observational Study.
papers.abstract: When trying to intervene early to prevent manic episodes, clinicians are hindered by patients underreporting their symptoms as they are becoming hypomanic or manic (ie, emerging symptoms). Continuous passive monitoring using wearable technology offers a potential solution to address this problem by capturing behavioral signals that do not depend on self-awareness. However, its clinical usefulness requires validation before implementation. This study aimed to evaluate whether passively collected wearable data can detect hypomanic symptoms using an explainable machine learning framework. We applied explainable machine learning to densely sampled multimodal data from a 2-year observational study of digital monitoring in 178 patients with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder (mean follow-up 540 days; range 120-706 days). Data on activity and sleep were collected continuously using wearable technology. Self-reported data were collected daily on their mood, energy, and anxiety, and weekly using the Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale (ASRM). To identify robust digital markers of hypomanic symptoms, we analyzed 252 time- and frequency-domain features from 43 participants who experienced at least 1 ASRM-defined symptomatic interval. Passively collected data achieved high accuracy, comparable with daily self-reported data in detecting symptomatic intervals (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.91 vs 0.93, respectively). Combined daily passive wearable data features achieved higher sensitivity (92.0% vs 85.4%), balanced accuracy (0.90 vs 0.89), and stronger rule-out usefulness (negative predictive value 97.8% vs 96.1%) than self-report data, with daily sleep features alone driving most of this signal (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.91, sensitivity 91.8%). The high classification performance using wearable data was explained by reductions in spectral entropy and flux across domains, reflecting a decreased complexity and variability in mood, activity, and sleep patterns, consistent with a shift toward pathologically stable states. Passive monitoring using wearable technology can detect hypomanic symptoms with high accuracy, supporting its potential as a clinically meaningful tool for continuous, objective monitoring in patients who underreport hypomanic symptoms. These findings are associative and concurrent in nature; they do not establish predictive validity. Prospective studies are needed to evaluate predictive validity for early detection of ASRM-defined symptomatic intervals.

papers.title: Frequency and Patient Throughput Characteristics of Implanted Cardiac Device Interrogation in the Emergency Department.
papers.abstract: Patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs), such as pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, frequently present to the emergency department (ED) with complaints potentially attributable to their devices. Device interrogation can characterize arrhythmias and guide management, but whether it represents a bottleneck to disposition has not been systematically studied. Retrospective cohort study at two academic centers (2024-2026). Visits were identified via consultations. Control cohorts of patients with general cardiology and EP consultations with pacemakers were propensity score matched. Intervals were compared via Kruskal-Wallis tests. Logistic regression investigated associations between demographic factors, time intervals, and admission. We identified 677 visits from 479 unique patients involving CIED-related EP consultation. The median ED length of stay (LOS) was 24.3 hours (IQR 10.2-36.1), with 80.4% admitted. General cardiology and EP consults without interrogation demonstrated similar times to consultation (4.0 [IQR 1.8-11.1] and 3.0 [IQR 0.9-12.4], p=0.4 and p=0.1), but shorter from consult to disposition (13.3 hours [IQR 12.7-14.4] vs. 5.2 [IQR 4.5-5.9] and 6.8 [IQR 6.0-7.5], both p<0.001). Consults with interrogation after hours were prolonged (14.9 [IQR 7.1-20.5] vs 7.1 [IQR 5.4-11.1], p<0.001). In the logistic regression, longer consultations were associated with higher likelihood of admission (aOR 1.05, 95% CI 1.02-1.07 per hour). No other factors were significant. Patients requiring CIED interrogation experienced delays relative to other patients, with interrogation as the proximate step before disposition. Consults after hours took longer, and delays were independently associated with admission. These findings highlight an operational bottleneck in acute CIED management, and efforts to expedite device interrogation warrant further investigation.

papers.title: Pearls & Oy-sters: Reversible Rapidly Progressive Dementia Associated With ASIA Syndrome Secondary to Silicone Implants.
papers.abstract: A 33-year-old woman with a medical history of polycystic ovary syndrome on combined oral contraceptive pills, insulin resistance, and bilateral silicone breast implants (SBIs) placed 10 years prior presented with a 2-month history of intermittent myoclonic jerks involving the head, trunk, and lower limbs; polyarthralgia; and cognitive and functional decline (compared with being previously independent in her activities of daily living). Family history was significant for epilepsy in her mother and 2 brothers. Neurologic examination revealed disorientation, significantly impaired short-term recall, visuospatial memory impairment, and a limited attention span. Her speech was characterized by frequent paraphasic errors and anomia; she also exhibited mild gait ataxia. Diagnostic studies ruled out common autoimmune diseases. Brain MRI and electroencephalography revealed no abnormalities, and CSF analysis was normal. Genetic testing for inherited prion disease and Huntington disease was negative, and serum and urinary copper levels were unremarkable. As part of a paraneoplastic workup, breast MRI revealed intracapsular rupture of both SBIs. The implants were surgically removed with complete capsulectomy. The patient's symptoms resolved completely by the seventh postoperative day. At the 6-month follow-up, she remained asymptomatic and had returned to her baseline functional status. Given the temporal association between implant rupture, explantation, and symptom resolution, the presentation was considered most consistent with a case of reversible rapidly progressive dementia secondary to the autoimmune/inflammatory syndrome induced by adjuvants.

papers.title: Association of a Structured Mindfulness-Based Nursing Intervention with Insomnia Severity and Emotional Distress in Patients with Comorbid Anxiety and Depression: A Retrospective Study.
papers.abstract: This single-center retrospective study examined whether receipt of a structured mindfulness-based nursing intervention (MBI) in addition to usual care was associated with lower insomnia severity and emotional distress than usual care alone. Inpatients admitted in 2025 receiving MBI plus usual care (n = 122) were compared with controls receiving usual care alone (n = 78). One-to-one propensity-score matching yielded 61 matched pairs, although residual imbalance remained in several baseline variables. Insomnia severity was measured using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), and emotional distress using the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale and 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. At discharge, the MBI group demonstrated significantly lower ISI scores (p < 0.001) with a 67.21% sleep response rate versus 31.15% in controls. After baseline adjustment, the MBI group showed greater reductions in anxiety and depression measures (both p < 0.001). The MBI group had fewer documented sedative-hypnotic orders and higher overall inpatient nursing satisfaction scores. Changes in ISI scores correlated significantly with changes in anxiety and depression. MBI allocation and higher baseline ISI independently predicted sleep response. A nurse-delivered structured mindfulness intervention was associated with greater reductions in insomnia severity and emotional distress in inpatients with comorbid anxiety and depression. Being retrospective, these findings indicate association rather than causation and require prospective confirmation.

papers.title: Behavioural sleep quality and quantity and their associations with age, salivary cortisol and abnormal behaviours: A preliminary field study in racing thoroughbreds.
papers.abstract: Sleep plays a key role in both physical recovery and welfare. However, sleep patterns remain poorly documented in animals, particularly in athletic horses. This study aimed to provide a detailed description of sleep quantity and quality in training Thoroughbred racehorses and to investigate their relationships with age, abnormal behaviours, and cortisol. Thirteen Thoroughbreds (2-7 years old) were continuously monitored in their home environment for 48 hours. An ethogram was used to quantify sleep-related behaviours associated with the two main behavioural sleep states: non-rapid eye movement (NREM-like) and rapid eye movement (REM-like), as well as sleep interruptions (from day 1 at 12:00 to day 3 at 12:00). Sleep Quality Indices (SQIs), reflecting the relationship between sleep duration and sleep interruptions (SIs), were then calculated. Behavioural observations of four indicators of poor welfare (alertness, stereotypies, inactivity, aggressiveness towards humans) were performed using scan sampling, and salivary cortisol was measured each morning. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess the links between sleep quantity and quality, age, mean cortisol, and abnormal behaviours. Age was significantly associated with behavioural sleep quantity, being positively associated with total behavioural NREM-related sleep (Wald test: χ2 = 5.40, p = 0.02), and negatively associated with total behavioural REM-related sleep (Wald test: χ2 = 4.36, p = 0.04) and total recumbency duration (Wald test: χ2 = 5.68, p = 0.02). Morning cortisol concentrations were negatively associated with Total SQI (Wald test: χ2 = 5.26, p = 0.02) and Combined SQI (Wald test: χ2 = 5.60, p = 0.02). Likewise, horses displaying abnormal behaviours more frequently had lower Total SQI (Wald test: χ2 = 4.07, p = 0.04), pointing to a potential link between stress or altered welfare and poorer sleep quality. These findings suggest that, whilst the type and duration of equine behavioural-related sleep may be mainly affected by age, sleep quality is associated with both cortisol levels and the expression of abnormal behaviours, indicating that poor sleep quality may be linked to poor welfare in this population of horses. Overall, these findings highlight behavioural sleep quality as a potential component of racehorse welfare assessment and warrant further investigation into the factors influencing sleep in athletic horses.

papers.title: Cross-modality Knowledge Transfer Between fMRI and EEG for Improved Single-modality Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) disrupts brain function in both spatial organization and temporal dynamics, which can be characterized by complementary fMRI and EEG measurements. In particular, fMRI provides higher spatial resolution to characterize multi-scale functional organization of brain networks, whereas EEG offers higher temporal resolution to capture dynamic neural activities across frequency bands. Thus, integrating the two modalities can characterize AD-related spatiotemporal disruptions more comprehensively than either modality alone. However, it is impractical to acquire paired fMRI and EEG data in real-world applications. To address this problem, we propose the fMRI-EEG Knowledge Transfer Network (FE-KTNet) to learn spatiotemporal representations from paired data and then transfer them back to modality-specific models through three stages. Specifically, in Stage 1, it learns modality-specific representations from fMRI and EEG FCNs, emphasizing multi-scale network organization for fMRI and frequency-specific electrophysiological coupling for EEG. Building on these representations, in Stage 2, it performs scale-wise bidirectional cross-modality fusion to integrate complementary information into fused multi-scale spatiotemporal representations. Finally, in Stage 3, it transfers the fused representations back to each modality-specific encoder through scale-wise feature alignment and logit-level knowledge distillation. We evaluate FE-KTNet on 14 multicenter datasets comprising 2,766 fMRI subjects and 1,842 EEG subjects, covering AD-NC, MCI-NC, and AD-MCI classifications. Compared with the corresponding baseline models, FE-KTNet increases fMRI-only and EEG-only accuracy by 3.4% and 6.1% for AD-NC classification, 5.2% and 8.0% for MCI-NC classification, and 3.5% and 7.1% for AD-MCI classification, respectively, and achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated methods. Our code is available at GitHub Repository.

papers.title: Neural Profiles of Pistol Shooting Performance Across Skill Levels in Hearing and Deaf Shooters: Insights into Cognitive-Motor Processes.
papers.abstract: Precision sport performance requires optimal motor preparation supported by efficient neural processing. While the psychomotor efficiency framework has been used to explain expertise-related neural patterns, it remains unclear whether such neural signatures generalize across individuals with different sensory experiences. The present study aimed to examine expertise-related neural oscillations during motor preparation in 10-m air-pistol shooting by comparing skilled and novice performers in hearing and deaf populations. Study 1 included 37 hearing participants (skilled: n = 19; novice: n = 18), whereas Study 2 included 43 deaf participants (skilled: n = 19; novice: n = 24). Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to assess temporal alpha asymmetry (T4 minus T3), parietal alpha, occipital alpha, frontocentral alpha, sensorimotor rhythm (SMR), and frontal midline theta during the 4 s preceding trigger pull. In Study 1, skilled hearing shooters showed lower temporal alpha asymmetry, reflecting relatively greater left temporal alpha power. They also exhibited higher posterior and frontocentral alpha power, a time-specific increase in SMR, and higher frontal midline theta power relative to novice shooters. In contrast, Study 2 revealed a distinct neural profile in deaf shooters. Deaf novices showed a time-dependent decrease in temporal alpha asymmetry as the trigger pull approached, whereas skilled deaf shooters remained relatively stable. In addition, skilled deaf performers showed reduced frontocentral alpha and SMR power relative to novices, indicating greater sensorimotor cortical engagement during motor preparation. These findings highlight population specificity in expertise-related neural profiles, indicating that neural markers of expertise may not generalize across sensory contexts. Rather than reflecting a universal pattern of psychomotor efficiency, the observed neural profiles may vary across populations with different sensory experiences. Overall, the present study highlights the importance of considering sensory experience when examining neural optimization and provides insights into the cognitive-motor processes underlying skilled performance across diverse athletic populations in precision sports.
papers.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

papers.title: Sleep pressure is increased by protein fragments and decreased by processive proteolysis.
papers.abstract: Sleep is universal among animals, yet the molecular-level causes and functions of sleep are incompletely understood. The fragment generation hypothesis (FGH) posits that sleep, at least in part, is an adaptive response to protein fragments, many of them protein-sized, that accumulate during wakefulness owing to cleavages by proteases, including caspases and Ca2+-activated calpains. According to the FGH, these fragments are a source of homeostatic sleep pressure that increases during wakefulness, and one function of sleep is to decrease protein fragment levels through their slower production and faster degradation during sleep. Predictions of the FGH have not previously been tested. Using zebrafish, we show that pharmacological inhibition of caspases decreases sleep, in agreement with the prediction of the FGH that a slower production of protein fragments would decrease sleep pressure. Pharmacological inhibition of the proteasome is shown to have the opposite effect, an increased sleep, in agreement with another prediction of the FGH, that sleep pressure would increase if fragments are protected from their proteasome-mediated degradation. Consistent with this prediction, a caspase-generated subunit of the activated caspase-3 is strongly upregulated by a sleep-increasing inhibition of the proteasome. The increase of sleep by proteasome inhibitors was found to be reduced by inhibition of calpains, suggesting that calpain-generated, proteasome-degradable protein fragments contribute to sleep pressure. Pharmacological inhibition of calpains also causes a decrease in rebound sleep after sleep deprivation, as predicted by the FGH. Together, these results suggest that the FGH may provide a molecular-level explanation of a cause and function of sleep.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

papers.title: Unraveling the Role of Sleep-Wake Cycle Regularity in Dementia Risk Assessment-Beyond Sleep Quantity.
Sleep-Wake Cycle Profiles and Incident Dementia and Cognitive Decline in Older Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep-wake cycle (SWC) disruptions are common in patients with dementia and potentially also in the preclinical phase of the disease. Accelerometers allow objective measures of multiple SWC dimensions: rest-activity rhythm (RAR), daytime activity, sleep, and chronotype, but these dimensions are rarely examined together. This study examined the association of SWC profiles, incorporating the 4 SWC dimensions, with incident dementia and cognitive decline. Prospective, UK population-based cohort study based on accelerometer data from the 2012 to 2013 wave of the Whitehall II cohort study, with a median (IQR) follow-up of 12.3 (12.0-12.7) years. Statistical analyses were conducted from June 2025 to March 2026. Participants were dementia-free aged 60 years or older with valid accelerometer data and covariates at baseline. Nine SWC profiles derived from 36 SWC metrics. Incident dementia cases until March 2025 were retrieved from electronic health records. Cognitive tests were administered in 2012 to 2013, 2015 to 2016, and 2019 to 2022 and each test score was standardized based on 2012 to 2013 data and all tests averaged to derive a global cognitive z score. Among 3973 participants (median [IQR] age = 68.4 [64.7 to 74.0] years; 26% women), 379 dementia cases were recorded during a median 12.3-year follow-up. Compared with participants with robust RAR (high level and amplitude, stable, not fragmented), light-intensity physical activity (PA) and good sleep (profile 3), those with poorer RAR (low level and amplitude, unstable, fragmented) along with low PA and poor sleep (profile 7), or with high level and low amplitude RAR and restless sleep (profile 8) had higher dementia risk (hazard ratio, 1.94 [95% CI, 1.32 to 2.84], and 1.96 [95% CI, 1.27 to 3.03], respectively). In analyses on cognitive decline (3806 participants), profile 7 as well as the most sedentary profile with the poorest RAR (profile 9) had faster 10-year cognitive decline (-0.14 [95% CI, -0.26 to -0.02]) and -0.28 [95% CI, -0.44 to -0.13], respectively). Cognitive outcomes in participants with robust RAR and higher PA were similar, irrespective of sleep. In this cohort study of 3973 older adults, consideration of all SWC dimensions was important in identifying profiles associated with cognitive outcomes; further studies are needed to evaluate whether SWC interventions reduce the risk or delay onset of dementia.

papers.title: Sleep-Wake Behavioral Analysis in Drosophila Using the Drosophila Activity Monitoring System.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease is associated not only with motor dysfunction but also with sleep-wake and circadian disturbances. Drosophila melanogaster provides a genetically tractable model for evaluating behavioral phenotypes relevant to Parkinson's disease. This chapter describes a protocol for quantitative sleep-wake behavioral analysis in adult Drosophila using the Drosophila Activity Monitoring system. Individual flies are loaded into glass activity tubes, and locomotor activity is recorded by infrared beam crossings, typically in 1-min bins. Sleep is defined as a period of 5 or more minutes of continuous inactivity. The resulting data can be used to calculate total sleep, daytime and nighttime sleep, sleep bout number, mean sleep bout duration, sleep latency, wake activity, and morning or evening anticipation behavior. This protocol provides a standardized approach for assessing sleep-wake phenotypes in Drosophila models of Parkinson's disease and for evaluating genetic, pharmacological, or environmental modifiers of sleep and circadian behavior.

papers.title: Electroretinogram Recording Using Drosophila Parkinson's Disease Models.
papers.abstract: The neuronal activity evoked by light stimulation is a useful indicator to evaluate early neural dysfunction. ElectroRetinoGraphy (ERG) is a relatively simple electrophysiological technique to measure these responses and is widely used in clinical settings, primarily for visual and optic nerve disorders, and has also been applied to the assessment of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease. In addition, ERG represents a highly useful and convenient research tool for studying neurodegenerative diseases using model organisms. In this chapter, we describe a protocol for ERG recording in Drosophila melanogaster, a well-established model organism in neuroscience research.

papers.title: Analysis of Dopaminergic Functions in Drosophila.
papers.abstract: Dopaminergic (DA) neurons regulate various physiological functions, including motor function, emotion, learning, sleep, and arousal. Degeneration of DA neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain causes motor disturbance in Parkinson's disease (PD). Studies on familial PD have revealed that a subset of PD genes encode proteins that regulate mitochondrial function and synaptic dynamics. Drosophila is a powerful model of PD, whereby genetic interactions of PD genes with well-conserved cellular signaling can be evaluated. Morphological changes in mitochondria, along with dysfunction and degeneration of DA neurons, have been reported in many studies using Drosophila PD models. In this chapter, we will describe imaging methods to visualize mitochondria in DA neurons and to evaluate spontaneous neural activity of DA neurons in the Drosophila brain.

papers.title: DISC-OSA: A European Delphi Consensus on OSA Screening in People with Obesity.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common among people with obesity (PwO) but remains frequently underrecognized and undertreated. The absence of harmonized screening frameworks in Europe leads to delayed diagnosis, preventable cardiometabolic complications, and increased strain on health systems. This study aimed to establish a Europe-wide expert consensus on the principles, target populations, and practical approaches to OSA screening in adults with obesity, thereby providing a structured framework to guide clinical and policy decisions. A two-round, modified mixed-methods Delphi study was conducted in accordance with the ACcurate COnsensus Reporting Document (ACCORD) 2024 reporting guidelines. A total of 20 draft statements across nine domains, informed by a pragmatic literature review, were considered by 26 multidisciplinary experts from European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) Collaborating Centres for Obesity Management. An independent Steering Committee oversaw governance and ethics. Consensus was defined as 70% or greater agreement and an interquartile range (IQR) of ≤ 1 on a 5-point Likert scale. All 20 statements met the predefined consensus criteria, particularly those emphasizing prioritization of PwO with cardiometabolic comorbidities, embedding screening within structured care pathways, and timely referral for diagnostic assessment. The STOP-Bang questionnaire was recommended as a first-line tool, with nocturnal oximetry or polysomnography as supplementary options. Consensus-endorsed statements informed a European consensus algorithm detailing who, how, and when to screen. This expert consensus provides a practical, scalable, and evidence-informed framework for systematic OSA screening within obesity care, supporting harmonized practice, early detection, and multidisciplinary management across European health care.

papers.title: Brainstem Circuits Engaged During REM Sleep Regulate Apnea Susceptibility.
papers.abstract: Breathing is dynamically regulated across sleep-wake states. However, how brainstem circuits support respiratory output during sleep, particularly during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, remains unclear. Here, we show that neurons in the preBötzinger Complex (preBötC), a core inspiratory rhythm generator, selectively exhibit elevated calcium activity during REM sleep. Inhibition of these neurons selectively increases apnea occurrence during REM sleep. Optogenetic activation produces state-dependent effects, inducing prolonged apnea during REM sleep and increasing the breathing rate during wakefulness. We further identify an upstream lateral parabrachial nucleus (LPBN) projection to the preBötC that showed related state-dependent effects. Inhibition of these preBötC-projecting LPBN neurons increases apnea susceptibility during REM sleep, whereas activation induces prolonged apnea during REM sleep. Together, our findings identify REM-engaged preBötC neurons and LPBN-preBötC projection-defined neurons, whose perturbation preferentially disrupts breathing during REM sleep. This state-dependent vulnerability may provide insights into the mechanisms that contribute to sleep-related respiratory disorders.

papers.title: Urinary incontinence and the impact on the quality of life of transwomen, travestis and non-binary people: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional study investigated the frequency of urinary incontinence (UI), its associated symptoms, and the impact on quality of life (QoL) in a sample of the trans and non-binary population. The study included 140 participants, divided into three groups: trans/transvestite/transfeminine women, trans/transmasculine men, and non-binary people, who answered the International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form (ICIQ-SF) and King's Health Questionnaire (Br-KHQ). The overall proportion of UI was 39.3%. Although the proportion was higher among trans women, transvestites, and transfeminine individuals (41.8%), non-binary people had the highest intragroup proportion (65%), reporting more frequent weekly losses, but in smaller amounts. Despite a better overall health perception, UI negatively impacted the personal relationships and emotions of non-binary participants. Specific symptoms, such as urgency, stress UI, and nocturia, were associated with adverse impacts on daily activities, relationships, emotions, and sleep/energy. It is concluded that UI is a frequent condition that significantly affects the QoL of trans and non-binary people, highlighting the need for clinical approaches sensitive to the specificities of each gender identity.

papers.title: Latent cortical network adaptability predicts dual-task-unmasked postural instability in Parkinson's disease: a proof-of-concept study.
papers.abstract: Dual-task postural deterioration often reveals latent balance vulnerability in Parkinson's disease (PD), even when single-task standing appears preserved. We examined whether beta-band cortical network solution-space organization during single-task standing predicts subsequent dual-task postural deterioration in PD. Forty-eight participants, including 16 healthy controls, 16 individuals with early-stage PD, and 16 individuals with mid-stage PD, completed single-task quiet standing and dual-task standing conditions while electroencephalography and center-of-pressure signals were recorded. Beta-band functional connectivity was estimated using the phase lag index, and minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was extended using an iterative second-best MST framework to characterize alternative backbone configurations based on cumulative MST cost divergence from the optimal MST (ΔCtotal(k)) and algebraic connectivity (λ2(k)). Dual-task-induced increases in postural sway became greater with advancing PD stage (p = 0.008), whereas conventional MST metrics showed no significant disease-stage trends. In contrast, dual-task standing induced stage-dependent solution-space alterations, with early-stage PD showing reduced ΔCtotal(k) and increased λ2(k), suggesting a more constrained alternative backbone configuration. Moreover, across participants, greater ΔCtotal(k) measured during single-task standing independently predicted larger dual-task-related increases in postural sway (ΔR2 = 0.048, p = 0.048) and greater reductions in postural complexity (ΔR2 = 0.115, p = 0.005), beyond baseline postural performance and disease group. These findings suggest that iterative second-best MST analysis may sensitively detect stage-dependent alterations in cortical network solution-space organization and provide a systems-level marker of dual-task postural vulnerability in PD.

papers.title: Image quality and procedural safety in neonatal brain MRI with and without sedation.
papers.abstract: Neontal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is susceptible to motion artefacts, whereas pharmacological sedation or anaesthesia may cause cardiorespiratory adverse events. We compared image quality and adverse events across three MRI strategies in newborns: natural sleep without sedation, pharmacological sedation, and imaging during mechanical ventilation. We retrospectively analysed 151 brain MRI examinations performed in a tertiary neonatal intensive care unit between August 2013 and August 2024. Examinations were classified as non-sedated using a feed-and-swaddle approach (n = 21), pharmacologically sedated without intubation (n = 67), or performed in intubated and mechanically ventilated infants (n = 63). Motion artefacts and documented adverse events were compared between groups. Motion artefacts were more frequent in non-sedated examinations than in sedated or intubated examinations (85.7% vs. 32.8% and 25.4%, respectively; p < 0.001). Moderate/severe artefacts occurred in 14.3%, 7.5%, and 0%, respectively. No adverse events were documented in the non-sedated group, compared with 8/67 (11.9%) in sedated and 7/63 (11.1%) in intubated infants; this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.275). Within the sedated cohort, artefacts were more frequent with chloral hydrate, whereas respiratory complications occurred predominantly with propofol-based sedation. Neonatal MRI strategies involve a clinically relevant trade-off between image quality and procedural safety. Natural-sleep MRI avoids pharmacological exposure and was not associated with documented adverse events but resulted in more motion artefacts. MRI strategies should therefore be individualized according to clinical condition and required diagnostic image quality. • Motion artefacts may compromise neonatal MRI, and pharmacological sedation or anaesthesia is frequently used to improve image quality. • Feed-and-swaddle MRI can avoid drug exposure, while sedative and anaesthetic agents may cause respiratory and haemodynamic adverse events. • Direct comparison of three real-world neonatal MRI strategies demonstrates a trade-off between image quality and procedural safety: sedation and controlled ventilation reduced motion artefacts, whereas no adverse events were documented during natural-sleep MRI. • Exploratory analyses suggest differences between sedation regimens, with more artefacts after chloral hydrate and respiratory events occurring predominantly with propofol-based sedation.

papers.title: The chronobiology of brain waste clearance: Sleep-wake and circadian regulation of glymphatic function.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system - a glia-dependent perivascular network mediating cerebrospinal fluid and interstitial fluid exchange - has emerged as a key determinant of restorative sleep, with its efficiency governed by both sleep-wake state and the circadian clock. Its activity peaks during NREM slow-wave sleep and is essential for clearing neurotoxic proteins including amyloid-β and hyperphosphorylated tau, whose accumulation underlies Alzheimer's disease and related neurodegenerative proteinopathies. This activity is itself under circadian control, with aquaporin-4 expression, CSF production, and perivascular flow exhibiting diurnal rhythmicity driven by the suprachiasmatic clock and peripheral clock genes. Recent work identifying synchronized norepinephrine oscillations from the locus coeruleus as the primary driver of glymphatic vasomotion has reframed the system's mechanistic architecture and raised questions about sedative-hypnotics and circadian disruption, both of which suppress this oscillatory pattern. This review synthesizes mechanistic, biomarker, and therapeutic evidence into a chronobiological framework positioning glymphatic efficiency as a distinct dimension of sleep quality - one that conventional EEG-based staging fails to capture. We examine disruption of glymphatic function by circadian misalignment, aging, sleep fragmentation, and neurodegeneration, and evaluate emerging biomarkers - including DTI-ALPS and plasma markers of waste accumulation - appraising their validity and limitations. Drawing on a broad literature survey and publication-trend analysis, we identify emerging perspectives to inform targeted therapeutic strategies. The therapeutic landscape is assessed across non-pharmacological, chronotherapeutic, pharmacological, and vascular and meningeal lymphatic interventions. We identify a translational gap between preclinical and human evidence, and propose that glymphatic biomarker endpoints be incorporated into sleep and chronobiology trials as a scientific priority.

papers.title: Influenza A-Associated Encephalitis and Encephalopathy in Adults: An Exploratory Criteria-Based Analysis.
papers.abstract: Influenza A can cause encephalopathy or encephalitis, yet adult data are scarce and the two entities are seldom distinguished systematically. This small retrospective study of five adults explored the feasibility and limitations of classifying these complications with the International Encephalitis Consortium (IEC) 2013 criteria and describes their clinical, radiological, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and treatment characteristics. We retrospectively reviewed five consecutive adults admitted to a tertiary center with polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-confirmed influenza A and acute neurological symptoms, all evaluated with brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), lumbar puncture, and electroencephalography (EEG). Encephalitis was defined by the IEC 2013 criteria (altered mental status > 24 h plus ≥ 2 minor criteria of central nervous system (CNS) inflammation). Data were analyzed descriptively. Three patients met criteria for encephalitis and two for encephalopathy (four women; age 44-68 years). Respiratory influenza A PCR was positive and CSF PCR negative in all. CSF pleocytosis occurred in two patients, bilateral thalamic and subcortical white matter MRI hyperintensities in two, generalized EEG slowing in four, and focal status epilepticus in one. All received oseltamivir; three received high-dose methylprednisolone, two of whom also required intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange. The categories overlapped substantially: EEG slowing and negative CSF PCR occurred in both, and treatment escalation followed clinical course rather than category, with the most intensive regimen required by one patient in each. At 3 months, three patients were asymptomatic and two, both with encephalitis and structural MRI lesions, had persistent deficits. In this small, hypothesis-generating study, IEC-based classification was feasible, but encephalitis and encephalopathy overlapped substantially and the distinction did not determine treatment. The main contribution lies in illustrating both the feasibility and limitations of criteria-based classification in adults with influenza A, rather than in establishing its clinical utility.

papers.title: When sleep and cognition measures diverge: a cross-source perspective on adolescent neurobehavioral research.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine

papers.title: Rasmussen's encephalitis in Turner syndrome needing a functional hemispherotomy-coincidence or connection?
papers.abstract: Rasmussen's encephalitis (RE) is a rare, chronic, immune-mediated epileptic encephalitis characterized by drug-resistant focal seizures, progressive unilateral cortical dysfunction, and hemispheric atrophy. Turner syndrome (TS), caused by complete or partial monosomy X, is associated with increased autoimmune susceptibility. The coexistence of RE and TS has not, to our knowledge, been previously reported; however, a single case can only raise the question of chance co-occurrence versus a biologically plausible immunogenetic connection. An eight-year-old girl with karyotype-proven TS presented with a two-year history of progressively worsening drug-resistant focal seizures. Serial MRI demonstrated progressive right hemispheric cortical atrophy, most pronounced in the frontal, insular, and mesial temporal regions, with right hemispheric hypoperfusion on arterial spin labelling. Video-EEG confirmed right frontocentral ictal onset without asynchronous contralateral onset. Despite immunotherapy, seizures persisted, and she underwent right functional hemispherotomy with seizure freedom at 8 months follow-up (Engel class I). We believe this to be the first reported coexistence of TS and RE. Although causality cannot be inferred from a single case, the observation supports discussion of X-linked immune dysregulation as a possible susceptibility factor in rare focal neuroinflammatory disease.
papers.journal: Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery

papers.title: Does Loneliness Condition the Association Between Restless Sleep and Later Depressed Mood? A Three-Wave Study of Korean Adults Aged 57 and Older.
papers.abstract: Sleep problems and loneliness are established risk factors for later-life depressive symptoms, but whether loneliness conditions their prospective association is rarely examined. Using three biennial waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2020-2024; N = 5,266; aged 57-98), we tested whether loneliness (2022) moderated the association between restless sleep (2020) and depressed mood (2024), each a single CES-D10 item, net of baseline depressed mood. Restless sleep (b = 0.063) and loneliness (b = 0.152) were each associated with later depressed mood, and their interaction was significant but small (b = 0.049, p = .011). The interaction was stable across added covariates and attrition corrections but was observed only with Wave 9 loneliness, was not reproduced with the CES-D8, and was inconsistent across ordinal thresholds. Later loneliness may flag older adults in whom restless sleep is more strongly linked to depressed mood; this evidence is tentative.
papers.journal: Journal of applied gerontology : the official journal of the Southern Gerontological Society

papers.title: Data-Driven EEG-fMRI Fusion: From Multimodal Integration to Latent Neural Inference.
papers.abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) capture neural dynamics across complementary temporal and spatial scales, but analyzing them jointly is difficult: the two modalities differ in measurement mechanisms, temporal resolution, and neurovascular coupling. EEG-fMRI fusion can be framed as an inverse problem, where the goal is to recover latent neural processes only partially observed through electrophysiological and hemodynamic signals. Here, we review data-driven fusion methods published between 2000 and 2025, focusing on techniques that identify shared neural representations across modalities. We organize methods by fusion strategies (symmetric vs. asymmetric), methodological objectives (factorization vs. translation), and modeling assumptions (linear vs. nonlinear), and discuss evaluation metrics and visualization strategies in current use. A recurring finding is the absence of a universal validation standard and the difficulty of interpreting latent multimodal components. Across neurological, psychiatric, and cognitive applications, EEG-fMRI fusion has revealed distributed network dynamics not accessible through unimodal analyses, though temporal misalignment, noise-induced coupling, and model-dependent interpretation remain persistent challenges. We close by discussing directions including nonlinear modeling, flexible coupling frameworks, and large-scale group-level fusion, and situate the field within a broader view of EEG-fMRI fusion as a problem of latent neural inference.

papers.title: Extreme delta brush as an ictal pattern in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
papers.abstract: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis frequently presents with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, and characteristic electroencephalographic (EEG) abnormalities including extreme delta brush (EDB). Differentiating epileptic from non-epileptic dyskinetic movements remains challenging, and the ictal versus interictal nature of EDB remains incompletely understood. In this case, a 22-year-old man developed neuropsychiatric symptoms progressing to hallucinations, confusion, abnormal speech, dyskinetic movements, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Brain MRI was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated positive anti-NMDAR antibodies. Continuous EEG initially showed diffuse slowing without correlation to dyskinetic movements of grimacing, jaw thrusting, and limb posturing. During treatment, abundant stereotyped episodes of facial pulling with rhythmic lip twitching emerged and were found on EEG to have an ictal correlate consistent with focal motor status epilepticus. Following reduction in ictal burden, EEG demonstrated a striking pattern of highly stereotyped right jaw movement and right arm internal rotation synchronized to complexes of midline beta-gamma activity overriding each delta wave peak, qualifying as a definite EDB pattern with clinical correlate to each EDB complex. Thus, in this case, EDB was an ictal pattern. This case illustrates the overlap between seizures and dyskinesias in anti-NMDAR encephalitis and highlights characteristic EEG findings including the EDB pattern. Unlike classic descriptions of EDB as a non-ictal EEG biomarker of severe anti-NMDAR encephalitis, this patient demonstrated clinical motor events time-locked to each EDB complex, supporting the possibility that EDB patterns represent ictal phenomena, at least in some cases such as this one. Continuous EEG monitoring is essential to distinguish electroclinical seizures from dyskinesias and may provide further insight into the potentially ictal significance of EDB.

papers.title: Electrophysiological "Brain Power" Dissipation: MEG Model-Dependent Power Estimates and Regional Metabolic Correlates.
papers.abstract: The human brain is often described as remarkably energy efficient, with its metabolic power consumption estimated at approximately 20 watts (W). Biophysical models partition this metabolic budget across cellular processes, including neuronal signaling. However, the electrical power dissipated by the synchronized cortical activity measurable with noninvasive electrophysiology remains unknown and should not be equated with total cortical energetic demand. Here, we used magnetoencephalography (MEG) source imaging of resting-state activity to estimate electrical power dissipation in cortical gray matter. Across 30 participants, mean total primary power summed over the modeled cortical source space was 6.6 × 10-9 W. We interpret this value as an empirical, model-dependent power estimate for the synchronized component of cortical activity accessible to MEG, rather than as an estimate of total cortical power. Targ‑eted sensitivity analyzes and order-of-magnitude checks suggested that the tested methodological choices could shift the estimate by approximately one to two orders of magnitude, but not enough to bridge the gap with metabolic benchmarks. Under a magnitude-based root-mean-squares approximation, finite-element estimates of secondary-current dissipation were approximately 30% of primary power in four central-tendency exemplars. Spatial patterns of MEG-derived power showed associations with PET-derived oxygen metabolism and transcriptomic maps of ketone metabolism, with heterogeneous effects across functional networks. These results define the scope and limitations of MEG-derived electrophysiological power estimates and motivate multiscale models linking synchronized electrical activity to regional metabolism.

papers.title: Validation of drug-resistant epilepsy identification algorithms in US Veterans across diverse care settings.
papers.abstract: Early recognition of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) is critical for timely referral to comprehensive epilepsy centers (CECs). Our prior pilot study in the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) demonstrated the feasibility of an algorithm-based approach to identify DRE within selected CECs. In this study, we validated and refined these algorithms in a broader, national cohort, including CEC and non-CEC care, to optimize algorithms for different care settings. We conducted a multicenter, retrospective study of randomly sampled veterans with epilepsy on ≥2 antiseizure medications (ASMs) from 1999 to 2024. Chart review by 26 epilepsy providers rated DRE status. Ninety-six candidate algorithms using combinations of six criteria-number of ASMs, treatment duration, dose thresholds, pregabalin exclusion, intractable International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes, and electroencephalography (EEG)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) utilization-were evaluated. Performance for DRE classification was evaluated among all veterans, and separately for CEC or non-CEC care. Among 970 veterans on ≥2 lifetime ASMs, 518 (53.4%) were rated as DRE, 363 (37.4%) as non-DRE, and 89 (9.2%) as undetermined. Veterans with DRE were younger (mean age = 68.9 vs. 72.0 years) and more frequently had at least one intractable ICD code (46.1% vs. 18.2%), EEG (77.8% vs. 66.7%), or MRI (78.0% vs. 65.8%) compared with non-DRE (all p-values <.001). Among all veterans, the best overall algorithm (area under the curve [AUC] = .701) identified DRE as either (1) exposure to 3+ ASMs or (2) exposure to two ASMs for at least 1 year, with the requirement of past EEG/MRI and intractable ICD code documentation. This algorithm was also highly effective among veterans who received CEC (AUC = .756) or only non-CEC care (AUC = .678). This national validation study confirms that medication-based algorithms can identify DRE within VHA administrative data across care settings (CECs and non-CECs). This supports the implementation of a standardized DRE definition for quality improvement, surveillance, and referral optimization within the VHA.

papers.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels.
papers.abstract: Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse's contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

papers.title: Non-hormonal management of menopause symptoms-the statement of the European Society of Gynecology.
papers.abstract: Menopausal symptoms, particularly vasomotor symptoms (VMS), sleep disturbances, mood disorders, and genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), affect a substantial proportion of women and may significantly impair the quality of life. Although menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) remains the most effective treatment, many women have contraindications to hormonal treatment or prefer non-hormonal options. To review and provide evidence-based recommendations on current non-hormonal interventions for the management of menopausal symptoms. The European Society of Gynecology convened an expert panel that performed a comprehensive literature review using MEDLINE and EMBASE. Clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, meta-analyzes, randomized controlled trials, and relevant primary studies evaluating non-hormonal interventions for menopausal symptoms were identified, critically appraised, and synthesized through a structured consensus process. Lifestyle modification, including healthy diet, regular physical activity, weight control, sleep hygiene, and behavioral interventions, forms the foundation of menopausal care. Among pharmacological therapies, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin, clonidine, oxybutynin, and pregabalin demonstrate varying degrees of efficacy for VMS. Neurokinin receptor antagonists, particularly fezolinetant and elinzanetant, represent the most effective evidence-based non-hormonal pharmacologic therapies currently available. Cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis effectively reduce VMS-related distress and improve sleep and quality of life. Evidence for complementary approaches such as mindfulness, yoga, acupuncture, acupressure, reflexology, phytoestrogens, S-equol, DT56a, purified pollen extracts, and black cohosh ranges from moderate to limited. For GSM, lubricants, moisturizers, hyaluronic acid preparations, and pelvic floor muscle training provide symptomatic benefit, whereas current evidence does not support routine use of vaginal laser therapy. Non-hormonal therapies provide effective and individualized treatment options for menopausal symptoms, particularly for women who are unable or unwilling to use MHT. Neurokinin receptor antagonists, selected pharmacologic agents, psychological interventions, and targeted GSM therapies represent the strongest evidence-based approaches currently available. The choice of treatment should consider symptom profile, contraindications, adverse effects, regulatory approval, and patient preferences.

papers.title: Sleep as a partial mediator of the association between residential greenness and biological ageing: A population-based study in China.
papers.abstract: Residential greenness has been associated with healthier ageing, but its relationship with sleep behaviours and the role of sleep in this association remain unclear. This study examined associations among residential greenness, sleep indicators, and biological age in middle-aged and older Chinese adults. This population-based study included 8,527 Chinese adults aged 45 years and older. Residential greenness was assessed using city-level normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI). Sleep indicators included night-time sleep duration, nap duration, total sleep duration, and categorical sleep measures. Biological age was estimated from chronological age and eight blood-based or physiological biomarkers. Multivariable regression and mediation analyses were used to examine the associations and potential mediating role of sleep behaviours. Higher NDVI was associated with lower biological age, with each 0.1-unit increase linked to a 0.529-year reduction. Longer night-time sleep was associated with younger biological age, whereas longer nap duration was associated with older biological age. Higher NDVI was modestly associated with longer night-time sleep and shorter naps. Mediation analyses indicated that night-time sleep duration, nap duration, and long naps partially mediated the association between NDVI and biological age, accounting for 2.7%, 5.7%, and 3.3% of the total effect, respectively. Residential greenness was associated with younger biological age. Sleep behaviours may partly explain the link between greener environments and healthier biological ageing.

papers.title: Atypical delusional misidentification with alternating impostors in a single body: a case report.
papers.abstract: Delusional misidentification syndromes (DMS), including Capgras and Fregoli syndromes, involve disturbances in identifying familiar individuals. Atypical presentations may challenge traditional classification and illuminate processes underlying familiarity and personal identity. A 42-year-old woman presented with persecutory and grandiose delusions alongside an unusual misidentification belief concerning her husband. Despite his unchanged physical appearance, she believed that different individuals alternately inhabited his body. She expressed complete conviction without insight, while remaining organised, fully oriented, and functionally independent. Neurological examination and routine laboratory and urine investigations were unremarkable. Neuroimaging, EEG, and formal neuropsychological assessment were not performed. Voluntary hospitalisation was offered but declined, and the patient was subsequently lost to follow-up. The presentation shares features with Capgras syndrome, through rejection of a familiar person as genuine, and Fregoli syndrome, through identity instability, but does not fully correspond to either. Unlike classical descriptions involving replacement or disguise, multiple identities were attributed to one physically unchanged familiar person. This may reflect a disturbed continuity of perceived personal identity rather than facial recognition alone. This case illustrates an atypical DMS presentation beyond traditional categorical definitions. Careful phenomenological characterisation of recognition, familiarity, and identity may help clarify atypical misidentification phenomena.

papers.title: Obesity is associated with alterations in the composition and function of the gut microbiota in patients with obstructive sleep apnea.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder marked by upper airway collapse, intermittent hypoxia, and sleep disruption. Growing evidence links gut microbiota dysbiosis to OSA-related complications, with obesity as a key risk factor. This study investigates the associations of OSA and obesity status with gut microbiota characteristics. Fecal samples were collected from 65 OSA patients and 15 healthy controls (HCs) and analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Clinical parameters, including body mass index (BMI), apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), lowest oxygen saturation (LSaO2), mean oxygen saturation (MSaO₂), and cumulative time with oxygen saturation below 90% (CT90), were also collected. Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) analysis, random forest, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression were employed to identify key microbial genera associated with OSA and obesity. Within the OSA cohort, subjects were stratified by BMI into obese OSA (Ob + OSA) and non-obese OSA (Non + OSA) groups to evaluate the association between obesity and the gut microbiota of OSA patients. The gut microbiota of OSA patients exhibited significant differences from that of healthy controls in terms of both community diversity and composition. LEfSe analysis, along with random forest and LASSO regression analyses, revealed a significant enrichment of Blautia, Fusobacterium, and the Eubacterium hallii group in OSA patients, while the abundance of Faecalibacterium was significantly reduced. Functional prediction analysis further indicated significantly enhanced activity in lipid metabolism and digestive system functions in OSA patients compared with healthy controls. Obese OSA (Ob + OSA) patients displayed differences in alpha diversity and the relative abundance of specific microbial taxa compared to non-obese OSA (Non + OSA) patients. The abundance of Synergistota was significantly higher in the Ob + OSA group than in the Non + OSA group, whereas the abundance of Blautia and Bifidobacterium was significantly lower. LEfSe analysis and LASSO regression identified increased Acidaminococcus, Megasphaera, and Morganella and decreased Anaerostipes and Lachnospiraceae UCG-004 as key characteristic genera distinguishing Ob + OSA from Non + OSA. Furthermore, obese patients exhibited more active functional pathways related to the metabolism of terpenoids and polyketides. The gut microbiota of OSA patients markedly differs from that of healthy controls, with obesity being associated with differences in microbial composition. Genera such as Blautia, the Eubacterium hallii group, and Faecalibacterium may serve as potential biomarkers for OSA, while Acidaminococcus, Megasphaera, Morganella, Anaerostipes, and Lachnospiraceae UCG-004 are characteristic of obese OSA patients. These microbial alterations may contribute to OSA pathogenesis and progression. This study provides further insight into gut microbial heterogeneity among OSA patients with different obesity statuses and provides a basis for future prospective and mechanistic studies. This study investigated gut microbiota characteristics in patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) according to their obesity status and compared these findings with those in healthy controls. By comparing obese and non-obese patients within the OSA cohort, we identified differences in microbial diversity and the relative abundance of specific taxa associated with obesity status. These findings provide further evidence of heterogeneity in the gut microbiota among OSA patients with different obesity statuses and may help inform future studies investigating the relationships among obesity, OSA, and the gut microbiota.

papers.title: Effects of High-Intensity Interval Training and Moderate-Intensity Continuous Training on Autonomic Regulation, Glycemic Control, and Health-Related Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus With Cardiac Autonomic Neuropathy: Study Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Cardiac autonomic neuropathy (CAN) is a life-threatening complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) characterized by impaired cardiovascular autonomic control. CAN significantly increases the risk of silent myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Exercise training is recognized as an effective non-pharmacological intervention for improving autonomic function; however, the comparative efficacy of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) in individuals with T2DM and confirmed CAN remains inadequately investigated. A three-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial will be conducted at the Centre for Physiotherapy and Rehabilitation Sciences and Dr. M. A. Ansari Health Centre, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi. Fifty participants with confirmed T2DM and CAN diagnosed using cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests (CARTs) based on Ewing's criteria will be randomized into HIIT, MICT, and control groups. Participants in the HIIT group will perform 4 × 4-min intervals at 85% to 95% of maximum heart rate (HRmax), 3 times weekly for 6 weeks. Participants in the MICT group will perform continuous treadmill training at 60% to 70% HRmax with similar frequency. Primary outcomes will include heart rate variability (HRV), heart rate recovery (HRR), and glycemic control. Secondary outcomes will include sleep quality, functional capacity, body composition, and health-related quality of life (HRQol). This study will provide evidence regarding the comparative effects of HIIT and MICT on cardiac autonomic modulation in T2DM patients with CAN. The findings may contribute to a better understanding of the effects of different exercise modalities on autonomic function, glycemic control, sleep quality, functional capacity, body composition, and HRQoL in this high-risk population. This trial has been registered with the Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI). CTRI/2026/02/104089. © 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC. Basic Protocol 1: Cardiovascular autonomic reflex testing Basic Protocol 2: Heart rate variability assessment Basic Protocol 3: Heart rate recovery assessment Basic Protocol 4: Glycemic control assessment Basic Protocol 5: Sleep quality assessment Basic Protocol 6: Functional capacity: 6-min walk test Basic Protocol 7: Body composition assessment Basic Protocol 8: Health-related quality of life: ADDQol-19.

papers.title: Chronotype, Mediterranean diet adherence, and FINDRISK score in adults: A cross-sectional mediation analysis.
papers.abstract: Chronotype has been linked to both dietary behavior and diabetes risk, but whether Mediterranean diet adherence statistically accounts for part of the association between chronotype and diabetes risk screening scores remains insufficiently characterized. In this cross-sectional study of 2,302 adults recruited via snowball sampling, chronotype was assessed using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ-19), Mediterranean diet adherence using the Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener (MEDAS-14), and diabetes risk using the Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (FINDRISK). Multiple linear regression and bootstrapped mediation analysis examined associations among chronotype, dietary adherence, and FINDRISK score, adjusting for age, BMI, and sex. MEDAS-14 scores increased progressively from evening-type to intermediate-type to morning-type participants (5.5 ± 1.4, 5.9 ± 1.5, and 6.4 ± 1.5, respectively; p < 0.001). After adjustment, higher MEQ-19 score was associated with higher MEDAS-14 score (β = 0.030, p < 0.001) and lower FINDRISK score (β = -0.021, p = 0.033), and higher MEDAS-14 score was independently associated with lower FINDRISK score (β = -0.162, p < 0.001). Mediation analysis identified a small but statistically significant indirect association between MEQ-19 and FINDRISK scores through MEDAS-14 (ACME = -0.005, 95% CI [-0.008, -0.002], p = 0.002). A small indirect association between chronotype and FINDRISK score through Mediterranean diet adherence was observed. Given the cross-sectional design and conceptual overlap between MEDAS-14 and FINDRISK, this finding should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in longitudinal studies using outcomes independent of the proposed mediator.

papers.title: Fibromyalgia: Update on Pathogenesis and Management.
papers.abstract: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a complex disorder characterized by chronic widespread pain, fatigue, sleep disturbances, mood alterations, and cognitive impairment. This review aims to provide an updated understanding of pathophysiology and management, highlighting recent advances in both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic treatment options. Multifactorial pathophysiology includes the central and peripheral nervous systems, psychosocial stressors, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the autonomic nervous system, and the immune system. Obesity and obstructive sleep apnea are also significant contributors. Diagnosis is clinical and requires a systematic approach. Nonpharmacologic treatments, including education, psychotherapy, exercise, and sleep optimization, are first-line management. Pharmacotherapy is offered to patients who need additional symptom control, and evidence for the most promising options is discussed. The review underscores the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to improve quality of life and suggests potential future directions for FM management. Cite this article as: Wu E, Brener A, Hiser JKD, Hill DLK, Farmer JO. Fibromyalgia: Update on pathogenesis and management. Eur J Rheumatol. 2025, 12(4), 0032, doi:10.5152/ eurjrheum.2025.25032.

papers.title: Lifestyle Modification Interventions as Therapeutic Adjuncts for Management of Prostate Cancer: A Mini-review.
papers.abstract: Prostate cancer remains a major global health challenge, and the antiandrogen toxicities associated with its management heavily reduce patient quality of life. Immunotoxic lifestyle habits, such as an unhealthy diet, inadequate sleep, and insufficient exercise, are major drivers of T-cell-mediated immune dysfunction in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) and cancers. Evidence demonstrates that lifestyle modification interventions acting as therapeutic adjuncts can reduce drug treatment requirements (DTRs), adverse effects, and organ toxicities in the management of IMIDs. While literature exists regarding how lifestyle modification may be used as a therapeutic adjunct for some IMIDs and cancers to reduce DTRs, adverse effects, and organ toxicities associated with their management drugs, there is currently none available for prostate cancer. Online searches were conducted across databases such as Google Scholar, PubMed, BioMed Central, and SciELO. Articles were reviewed using keywords such as prostate cancer, lifestyle modification, therapeutic adjuncts, and immune dysfunction. As adjunctive therapeutic strategies for prostate cancer care, lifestyle modification interventions could potentially reduce antiandrogen DTRs, costs, adverse effects, and organ toxicities.

papers.title: Polycystin Dysfunction and Cardiac Electrical Abnormalities in ADPKD.
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is one of the most common inherited kidney disorders characterized by the progressive formation of renal cysts. It is a systemic disease with significant extrarenal manifestations. Among these, cardiac electrical abnormalities are increasingly recognized as clinically important yet underappreciated contributors to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Beyond cyst formation, pathogenic variants in PKD1 or PKD2, which encode polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, respectively, interfere with calcium homeostasis, mechanotransduction, and mitochondrial function in both kidney and heart tissues. These molecular changes trigger a cascade of pathological events, including renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation, transforming growth factor-driven fibrosis, and oxidative stress, leading to structural and electrical remodeling of the heart. These alterations contribute to cardiac electrical remodeling, manifesting clinically as QT interval and corrected QT (QT/QTc) prolongation, left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, and other electrocardiographic abnormalities. Despite growing evidence, cardiac electrical abnormalities in ADPKD remain understudied in clinical practice. Early detection of subclinical cardiovascular abnormalities may be facilitated by electrocardiographic monitoring, cardiac imaging, and complementary biomarker assessment. Additionally, findings from iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte models support the translational potential of personalized drug-screening platforms. This review summarizes current evidence linking polycystin dysfunction to cardiac electrical abnormalities in ADPKD by integrating molecular mechanisms with experimental and clinical findings. It also highlights the need for integrated cardio-renal approaches to improve cardiovascular surveillance, risk stratification, and future therapeutic development in ADPKD.

papers.title: Perioperative methadone: Clinical use and knowledge among Australian anaesthetists.
papers.abstract: Intravenous methadone has re-emerged as a perioperative analgesic, yet uncertainty persists regarding its optimal use. Variation in clinician practice and interpretation of pharmacological principles may influence its safe and effective application. We conducted a mixed-methods survey-based study within a national anaesthesia educational programme (ADVANCE). A voluntary, anonymous pre-presentation clinician survey was distributed to predominantly Australian anaesthetists to characterise methadone use, dosing strategies, adjunct prescribing and patient selection. Real-time audience polling during the educational session assessed clinician responses to pharmacology-based and clinical decision-making scenarios. Survey and polling datasets were analysed independently using descriptive statistics. A total of 726 clinicians completed the survey. Overall, 50.6% (n = 367) of respondents reported using methadone. Among users (n = 367), practice varied widely across surgical contexts and dosing strategies, including weight-based, fixed and procedure-dependent approaches. Concurrent administration of additional opioids and central nervous system depressants was common (86.1%). Clinicians reported avoiding methadone in specific patient groups, most frequently frail patients, those with prolonged QT interval, or obstructive sleep apnoea. Polling responses demonstrated variability in clinician interpretation of pharmacological principles, particularly regarding timing of central effects. Perioperative methadone use is characterised by substantial variation in uptake, dosing and adjunct prescribing. Variability in clinician responses relative to pharmacological reference data, combined with frequent co-administration of additional opioids and sedatives, highlights potential areas for targeted education and institutional safeguards to support safe implementation.

papers.title: Heart rate variability, sleep quality, and quality of life in epilepsy patients are multidependent and cannot be reduced to the quality of seizure control.
National Trends and Demographic Disparities in Self-Reported Cognitive Difficulty Among U.S. High School Students, 2015-2023.
papers.abstract: The National Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) asks students whether, because of a physical, mental, or emotional problem, they have serious difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions. We analyzed nationally representative 2015-2023 YRBS data from 50,222 U.S. high school students using survey-weighted prevalence estimates and logistic regression. The prevalence of this self-reported cognitive difficulty increased from 29.9% (95% CI, 27.7%-32.1%) in 2015 to 45.0% (95% CI, 43.1%-47.0%) in 2023-approximately 3 in 10 students to nearly 1 in 2 (adjusted odds ratio per 2-year cycle, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.18-1.25)-while 2021 and 2023 estimates were similar. The increase was steeper among female than male students. In secondary models, insufficient sleep, excessive recreational screen use, frequent poor mental health, household basic needs not consistently met, and unstable housing were associated with cognitive difficulty. These findings identify a growing functional signal requiring surveillance, school-health assessment, referral pathways, and further study.
papers.journal: The Journal of school nursing : the official publication of the National Association of School Nurses

papers.title: Psychological Assets and Cardiovascular Health in Adulthood: A Mixed Methods Investigation.
papers.abstract: Psychological risk factors like depression increase risk for poor cardiovascular outcomes but psychological assets like purpose in life are protective and linked to reduced risk of cardiovascular events. However, most assets are investigated individually, and not all have been explored in relation to cardiovascular health (CVH). This study used mixed methods to assess multiple psychological assets and evaluate associations with CVH 12 years later. Data came from 2092 participants in the National Child Development Study. At age 50 years, participants wrote open-ended responses describing their futures. Two trained researchers qualitatively coded each response by rating them for 7 commonly assessed psychological assets (1=not at all; 7=very): optimism, purpose, satisfaction, personal growth, agency, enjoyment, and overall positivity. At age 62, CVH behavioral factors (exercise, smoking status, sleep) were self-reported; CVH clinical factors (blood pressure, lipids, glucose, body weight) were measured during nurse visits. Following Life's Essential 8 guidelines, CVH components were combined into total CVH scores. Linear regressions examined associations between each age 50 asset and age 62 CVH scores, adjusting for age 50 confounders. All age 50 assets were positively associated with better CVH scores 12 years later, accounting for sociodemographic characteristics and word counts (p≤0.05). Purpose (b=0.81 [95% CI, 0.33-1.29]) and personal growth (b=0.82 [95% CI, 0.34-1.20]) showed the strongest associations with CVH in fully adjusted models. Higher levels of most midlife psychological assets were linked with better CVH over time, suggesting multiple paths to health protection. These findings highlight assets that could be prevention targets.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

papers.title: Associations between daily university belonging, imposter syndrome and ethnic/racial sleep disparities among first-year college students: A daily diary assessment.
papers.abstract: The transition to college presents significant life changes in social dynamics and academic demands, all of which can affect students' sleep. Using a longitudinal lens, we examined how daily assessments of university belonging and imposter syndrome were associated with sleep. Five hundred eighty-three first-year college students (Asian = 23.6%, Black = 14.1%, Latinx = 30.6%, White = 29.2%, Other = 2.6%) at a private university in the Northeast United States participated in this study. Students completed a 14-day daily diary assessment in the Fall semester (T1) and completed a follow-up survey in the Spring semester (T2). Results revealed that both mean levels and variability of daily university belonging and imposter syndrome during Fall semester were associated with sleep outcomes one semester later, after controlling for demographic and environmental covariates and prior sleep. Higher mean-levels of daily university belonging across 14 days were associated with earlier bedtime and better sleep quality one semester later. In contrast to mean-level university belonging, higher mean-levels of daily imposter phenomenon across 14 days were associated with later bedtime and greater daytime dysfunction. Furthermore, greater variability in daily imposter syndrome across 14 days was associated with later bedtime and longer sleep latency one semester later. Promoting a sense of university belonging, assessing imposter syndrome, and taking into account the daily-level variability in these constructs promptly in the beginning stages of the college transition may be beneficial for students' sleep outcomes.
papers.journal: Journal of diversity in higher education

papers.title: Understanding Sleep in Ultramarathon Runners: An Exploratory Assessment during a Training Week.
papers.abstract: Sleep plays a vital role in sports performance. Ultramarathon runners may experience impaired sleep during training and competition; however, further investigation is needed. The current study aimed to evaluate sleep in ultramarathon runners during a typical training week. We evaluated 15 male athletes with a mean age of 45.1 ± 10.5 years and a mean ultramarathon experience of 6.37 ± 6.49 years. Sleep was assessed using the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire, the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, the Athlete Sleep Behavior Questionnaire, the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, and a 7-day sleep diary. Most participants were morning chronotypes (86.7%), and the mean social jetlag of was 0.60 ± 0.69 hour. The athletes went to bed and woke up earlier on workdays than on free days ( p = 0.002). Most athletes reported < 8 hours of sleep per night, 53.3% reported poor sleep-related behaviors, and 46.7% were classified as poor sleepers; however, 73.3% did not report excessive daytime sleepiness. These findings suggest a heterogeneous and multidimensional sleep-health profile in ultramarathon runners.

papers.title: Identifying characteristics and behavioral phenotypes of musculoskeletal disorders using wearables in All of Us.
papers.abstract: Wearable devices provide continuous measures of daily activity, sleep, and heart-rate (HR)-derived characteristics, creating new opportunities for digital phenotyping of musculoskeletal disorders (MSD). However, longitudinal behavioral patterns and heterogeneity among individuals with MSD remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify characteristics associated with MSD and characterize behavioral phenotypes using longitudinal wearable data. We analyzed 2344 participants (MSD = 1036; non-MSD = 1308) from the All of Us Research Program. First, supervised machine-learning models were trained using sociodemographic, physical measurement, and wearable-derived features to distinguish individuals with and without MSD and identify factors associated with MSD status. Model interpretation was performed using SHapley Additive exPlanations values. Second, temporal profiling and unsupervised clustering were applied to 90-day wearable trajectories of participants with MSD to identify behavioral phenotypes. XGBoost achieved the best classification performance (accuracy = 0.929, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve = 0.930, area under the precision-recall curve = 0.870, F1 = 0.919). Important factors associated with MSD included lower activity, longer sleep, and female sex. Behavioral phenotyping identified 5 distinct phenotypes differing in activity patterns, sleep characteristics, HR-derived measures, pain burden, mental health conditions, and employment status. Notably, high-pain phenotypes exhibited greater prevalence of anxiety and depressive disorders, lower pulse rate variability, and distinct sleep profiles compared with more active phenotypes. These phenotypes demonstrated moderate reproducibility in bootstrap-based stability analysis (mean adjusted rand index = 0.62).
